s01.slug: THURSDAY · 12:15 PM · ANACAPA COMMONS — THE WINDOW TABLE
body: It is the first dry Thursday since the storms, and the window table in the Commons has the sun on it end to end, a long yellow slab of January, the first in two weeks that anyone could sit in. The glass is warm enough to lean on. Out on the lawn the bike racks are steaming, and a girl in a Serra Hall sweatshirt has carried an entire mattress pad outdoors to dry and stands over it with her arms folded.

Jack comes straight from Oceanography, where Skye spent the hour in the back row under the exit sign and left at the bell for a hair appointment in Montecito that Corinne booked, and he is hungry. Kevin is there first. His tray is lined up with the edge of the table, his BlackBerry lies face down beside the napkins, and next to a plate of eggs he hasn’t touched are two index cards: one soft at the corners from a week in a shirt pocket, one new and white, filled to the margins in his small careful letters.

body.text: “You asked me to hold you to something,” Kevin says, before Jack has set down his tray. “I’m holding.” He moves the second chair out from the table with his foot.
body.else: Kevin asked him in the hall last night: lunch, Thursday, the window table, *I have a list*. Now, before Jack has set down his tray, he moves the second chair out from the table with his foot.

body: By the cereal bar the Louisiana table has hung a gold ribbon on the milk dispenser and is on its third *Who dat?* since Jack came in, ten days out from Miami, with the waffle line answering. Jack’s eyes stay on Kevin’s cards. The cereal bar is a cereal bar.
“Before the list,” Kevin says, and lays his fork in the groove of the tray. “Laney told Margot. Margot told me. I asked her not to, and she said it was a public-health matter.”

body.text: “I’m not taking a side. I don’t have the information and I don’t want it.” He turns the new card face down. “Just — you were both on my list for the van. I’d like to never have to make that list again.”
body.else: “Evan said the dog shook.” He turns the new card face down. “I’m a dog person. That’s all I’ve got.”

body: “It’s done, Kev.”

Kevin looks at him across the two cards. He turns the new one face up again and picks up his fork. Jack is hungry in a plain, uncomplicated way, and the eggs are good: the Commons runs breakfast all day on Thursdays, for reasons lost to history, and somebody in the back has finally learned what butter is for.

Margot comes by the window table with a hot water and one piece of dry toast, in the black she wears for grief and for everything else, and does not slow down to deliver it. “Salinger’s dead. Ninety-one. New Hampshire.” She tips the toast toward the register, where a girl in a Lit sweatshirt has her face in a bagel. “The *Times* had the obituary ready, which tells you something about the *Times*.”
“Was he Catholic?” Kevin asks.
“He was everything for about a year each.” She sets a napkin at the Lit girl’s elbow without breaking stride and carries the rest of her breakfast to a table by herself, with her back to the room.
“That’s her version of a sympathy card,” Kevin says, low, of the napkin. “She’ll say it was sanitation.”
Doug goes by with two trays and a hash brown in his mouth, takes in the cards over Kevin’s shoulder, and says “Dude” with feeling. “Just tell her you like her violin.”
“I do like her violin,” Kevin says. “It’s item one.”
“Then you’re done,” Doug says, and carries his trays off to a table in the sun with a man’s total confidence, and Kevin watches him go. “He’s right,” he says. “It’s the worst thing about him.”
“So,” Kevin says, and taps the new card, and Jack watches him become an attending. “Hour four. Presentation of the problem.”

He lays it out in order of severity. The first hour of any encounter is the history and physical; hours two and three are the procedure; hour four is recovery, and he has never been handed a script for recovery. The Walk van was six hours and Clare slept five of them: not a problem, but data. Javi has invited him to a Niners game in the fall, with the family, an offer Kevin describes as a standing order: nine hours door to door, the tailgate and the game and the drive back down 280, and somewhere in the third quarter, with four brothers on one side of him and the thermos empty on the other, there is an hour when no one is being introduced to anyone and the prepared material has run out. “One through three, I’m great,” he says. “I have the handshake.”
“The long normal one.”

“It’s a long normal one,” Kevin says, with dignity, “and I’ve worked on it.” He holds out his hand across the table to prove it, and Jack takes it: three seconds, eye contact, no pump. It comes back to Jack feeling reviewed.
“Nine out of ten,” Jack says. “Lose the left hand on the elbow. That’s a county commissioner.”
“It’s *warm*.”
“It’s a county commissioner.” Kevin takes his left hand off his own elbow and looks at it.
Kevin turns the new card around and slides it over, and Jack reads it with a forkful of egg held in the air.

body.title: Index card, in Kevin’s hand
body.text:
THINGS TO SAY AT HOUR FOUR

1. Her violin (chin rest? NOT the sound)
2. Her brothers: four. Names, in order (J, L, N, T)
3. The Walk — how are her knees
4. “Do you like the 9:30 or is it a family thing”
5. Niners, 9–7 last year (verify)
6. The measure with which you measure (today’s Gospel — too much?)
Under the Gospel, one more line has been crossed out once and written over in the same small letters: *Thank Skye (via Jack).*

body: “Why not the sound?” Jack asks, at the first line.

“Because I can’t tell a good one from a bad one,” Kevin says, “and she knows it. She told me hers was her grandfather’s, a Czech violin, and I said *wow*, and she said, *You don’t know anything about violins*, and I said *No*.” He looks happy. “It was the best moment of the Walk.”
“Eight and eight,” Jack says, and taps the fifth line. “Last year. The Niners. They were eight and eight.”
Kevin looks at the line. “Clare would know that.”
“Clare would know that.”

He crosses out *9–7* with one ruled stroke, writes *8–8* over it, and says, with feeling, “This is why I need a second reader.” He taps the sixth line. “The Gospel today is the lamp on the lampstand, and the measure you give being the measure you get. I went to Mass this morning. It’s Aquinas’s feast, and it was in my head. Too much?”
“For a Niners game?”
“For a Niners game with her *brothers*.”
“Too much.”
“I knew it,” Kevin says, happier than he has been all lunch, and does not cross it out. He uncaps the pen. “Be honest. Where does it fall over?”

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. I told Priya I was out. He erased it. Tuesday at four I woke him for Doug. A chair under the knob, then a bell. Wednesday at the Brick, at the next carrel all night: ‘You two have been defending each other for three hours. That isn’t studying.’ Sings bass. A real one. Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose — his mother made him. Friday, from the Odyssey: Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something. Back from San Jose. His mother has a girl from their parish she wants him to call. Clare. She plays the violin in the Mass band. Wednesday he brought two flats of water to the Haiti table, which nobody asked for, and stayed to hold Clare’s violin case. ‘My mother knows your mother.’ Thursday he called Clare. His mother had the number, and his grandmother was on the speaker. She said yes to Sully’s. MLK Day he brought gloves for everybody. Tuesday in the basement he read us the first reading off his BlackBerry. Clare’s going to the Walk for Life, and so is he. He asked me to come — for him. I said yes. Thursday at the window table he had a list: things to say at hour four. He’d heard about Hale’s — Laney to Margot to him — and didn’t take a side.

choices.text: *Tell him what hour four is actually like.*
choices.key: At the window table Kevin asked what you’re supposed to feel at hour four. You told him what it’s actually like. He wrote it down.
response: Jack puts the fork down. It turns out there is an hour-four speech in him that he hasn’t been told about, and it comes up whole.

“You stop listening for your turn,” he says. “That’s first. You’ve been holding your next sentence for three hours, and somewhere in there you notice you dropped it, and you’re just listening, and what she’s saying is better than what you had. Then you find out you’ve been arguing for an hour about a book you can’t stand, and you’d pick it up again tomorrow to keep going. And you look at the clock, and it’s later than you thought, and all you want is for the drive home to be longer.” He hears himself stop. “That’s hour four, Kev. You want the drive to be longer.”

Kevin has been writing it down. Word for word, in the small careful letters, across the white card at the speed of Jack’s voice, and somewhere around *the drive* the pen quits and rests on the paper. He reads it back to himself once, carefully, like a label.
“Okay,” he says, brightly. “Seven out of ten pre-meds would have said *comfortable silence*. I was going to say *comfortable silence*.”
“It’s a good answer, *comfortable silence*.”
“It’s the answer of a man with a list,” Kevin says.
He caps the pen, folds the white card once, and slides it into his shirt pocket behind the old one.

choices.text: *Be Clare. Be a better Clare than Clare.*
choices.key: At the window table you played Clare for Kevin — badly, then well — so he could practice hour four on you.
response: “Give me your Niners cap,” Jack says.
Kevin has it in his backpack, folded in thirds like a flag. Jack puts it on backward and becomes Clare Dominguez.

He does her badly first. His Clare has a voice from somewhere between a game-show contestant and Margot, and she holds an invisible violin like a cello and saws at it from the elbow, and Kevin, wounded, says, “She doesn’t do the elbow,” and Jack drops an octave, hunches over an invisible playbook, and says, “Third and long, Kevin. What’s the formation?”
“Pray?” Kevin says.

Jack, as Clare, lowers the playbook and only looks at him, patient, with ten thousand dinners in it, until Kevin says, “It’s a nickel package, I think, they’ll have a safety in the box —” and runs down, because the girl across the table has started to smile at him and is not being unkind about it.
“You don’t have to ask about my brothers, Kevin,” Clare says, low and amused and not doing any elbow at all. “They’re going to ask about you. Javi already has a folder.”
Kevin laughs, a real one, and forgets the bit entirely and answers her. “I said *Honorable, sir*.”
“You did.”
“He told me not to call him sir.”
“He likes you.”
“Do you think —” Kevin stops. He takes the cap off Jack’s head by the bill and holds it in both hands. “Out of character. What are you supposed to feel at hour four? Actually.”

Jack gives it to him out of character too, shorter and with less on it. “That you’ve stopped keeping score. That you’d rather be bored with her than entertained by anybody else, and you aren’t bored. That you want the drive to be longer.”

Kevin writes it on the back of the white card, and his pen slows on the last line and writes it smaller than the rest. Then he turns the old card face up, the one with *Thurs. — hr 4* copied onto it in the small careful letters, and puts a check mark after it. “That was the ask,” he says, and sets the cap on his own head, forward, as God intended.

response: “That’s the list,” Kevin says, and looks at his watch. “So I have fifty-eight minutes and twenty seconds I haven’t planned.”

He turns the white card over. At the bottom of the back a line has been ruled in pen, and nothing is written on it. “This one I couldn’t write.” He is looking at the ruled line. “What are you supposed to feel? At hour four. I have the questions. No one told me what it’s supposed to be.”

s02.slug: THURSDAY · 3:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — THE TIE
body: The iron has been going ten minutes. 412 does not own an ironing board and Theo has declined to believe in that, so the shirt is laid across a towel on the lid of Jack’s footlocker, and Theo irons as he does everything he was never taught, at a speed that implies mastery, back and forth over the same collar. On the windowsill his speaker is playing a record from 1982 on which a saxophone sounds like money.

There is no seminar. Hale is in New York today, according to the Philosophy Department’s e-mail, to which Theo has subscribed himself along with every other list the department keeps (“the last epistolary novel in print”), and he has translated the notice aloud twice already: “*On a matter of public disputation* means being rude to a churchman on a stage, for money.” Jack has the afternoon, and Gloria has given him the night off for it, with a look. He has a suit to be pinned into.

It is the only one of Theo’s suits that Jack’s shoulders will go into, a charcoal, and it goes on over them. Below the belt it is Theo’s. Theo is four inches taller and is kneeling at Jack’s ankles with two of Priya’s safety pins, taken from a laminated EMERGENCIES envelope on her door in a transaction Priya has not yet been informed of.
“Hold still,” he says. “You are a hem in motion.”
“Is this an emergency?”
“Look at your trousers.” On the nightstand Hollis presides from his teacup, retired with honors.
“How do I walk in these?”
“Like you own the trousers,” Theo says, through the second pin. “They’ll believe you.”
When the hem is done he does the shoes, Jack’s own black ones from the Mooney spring formal. 412 has no brush, so he works the polish in with a sock pulled over his fist, and the sock is Jack’s.
The RAZR goes off on the desk at 3:31.

body.text: wear the tie he picks. not the one you like. i will explain nothing

body: “Read it again,” says Theo from the floor, so Jack does, and Theo nods at the shoe. “*Not the one you like.* I have known that girl a very long time, and I want it noted that she has never once been wrong about a tie.”
“It’s a fundraiser in the Palisades,” Jack says. “That’s all I’ve got. Her publicist says it’s civic.”

“Everything in Los Angeles is civic, Costigan. It’s how they get the parking.” Theo gets up off his knees, takes a navy silk off the closet door, and goes to the full-length mirror, where he knots it on himself for the lesson. “There are three honest knots,” he says. “The four-in-hand is for the young and the guilty. It’s lopsided, it’s loose, it looks like you got dressed in a moving car, and the world forgives you. The Windsor is for men who have been photographed. A half-Windsor is a *commitment*, Costigan. Like a coat.”
“And the fourth knot?”

“There isn’t a fourth knot. There are men who want to be asked about their knot.” The navy goes over, under, through. “Lapels next. The lapel is the only part of a jacket with a point of view. Pocket square: no. A pocket square is a cry for help in silk.” He reaches across and settles Jack’s lapel with a thumb. “You look like a man someone would vouch for, Costigan. It’s a dreadful risk.”

In the mirror, over Theo’s shoulder, the open door of 412 shows a slice of the hall, and a pink BlackBerry goes across it at hip height and stops. Laney is above it in a quilted vest and full makeup, one hand on the doorframe, her mouth open on the beginning of something. It lasts a second. Theo’s hands stop on the knot. The pink BlackBerry goes on down the hall toward the stairs, and the slice of hall is only a hall. Jack, trousers pinned, is looking at his own cuff.

body.text: It takes Theo a moment to find the knot again. When he has it up to his collar he says it to the knot: “You were good at it. Wednesday. That’s what I didn’t like.” He gives the silk a last tug. “One question, and then I’ll dress you in silence. The phone call, in January. What did she actually say?”
“Pick a tie,” Jack says.
Theo lets it be picked. He slides the navy off over his head, still knotted, and drops it on the bed.

Theo knots and unknots the navy twice more and says nothing about Wednesday, and the nothing is the loudest thing in 412. “Pick a tie,” he says. He slides it off over his head, still knotted, and drops it on the bed.

body: Beside it on the bedspread lie the two candidates. Theo’s is a dark green knit that, he says, *says I read*. The other is the red silk Ma bought at the Southern Park Mall for Christmas Mass, the best thing Jack owns, worn exactly once.

choices.text: *Hold up the one you like.*
response: Jack holds up the red one.
Theo takes it by the tail and studies it at arm’s length. “That tie is a confession, Costigan. Your mother bought it for a Christmas Mass in Ohio. It wants to go home.”
“It’s a good tie.”
“It’s a great tie for a boy in a pew. Tonight you’re a boy in a room.” He hangs it back on the closet door and smooths it straight, and the green goes on.

He ties it on Jack himself, from behind, both of them facing the mirror, a half-Windsor, quick and tight, the saxophone sliding along somewhere in the room. He turns Jack by the shoulders to see the result.
“Don’t agree with anyone,” he says.

choices.text: “You pick. She said you’d know.”
response: Theo doesn’t look at either tie. “That is either the nicest thing you’ve ever said to me or a delegation of authority,” he says. “Either way I accept the commission.” He lifts the green off the bedspread, stands Jack in front of the mirror, and ties it on him himself, a half-Windsor, very fast, and for once doesn’t narrate it. The only sounds in 412 are the saxophone and the silk being drawn up through itself. He draws the knot up to a finger’s width from the collar button and sets it with his thumbs. “Snug enough to feel,” he says. “Loose enough to leave.” He steps back.
“Don’t agree with anyone, Costigan,” he says, gently, and hangs the red one back on the closet door, where it can wait.

choices.text: *Let him do the whole speech.*
response: “Go ahead,” Jack says, and sits on the edge of the bed with his hands between his knees, and Theo gives him all of it.

There are the dimples. There is the gorge of a lapel, demonstrated on Jack’s own jacket with a finger, and the long sad history of the Duke of Windsor, wrong in two particulars and delivered flawlessly, and a digression on why no man who has ever worn a tie clip has had a happy ending. Jack sits through all of it, because the end is where Theo is happiest, and the clock on the RAZR can do what it likes.

By the time the green is on, a half-Windsor, tight and symmetrical, the RAZR says 4:38. Theo turns Jack to the mirror by the shoulders. “Don’t agree with anyone,” he says. Two minutes later a horn goes twice down at the curb, and Theo’s hands come off Jack’s shoulders.

s02a.slug: THURSDAY · 4:40 PM · US-101 SOUTH → PACIFIC COAST HIGHWAY — THE SAAB, TOP UP
body: By the Rincon the sun is down level with the soft top, coming in flat off the water under the visor, and it lays a stripe of gold across the dash and the backs of Skye’s hands at the top of the wheel. Out past the point the surfers sit their boards in a loose row, waiting on a set. The iPod rides on its cord in the cup holder, and a boy on it is singing over cheap bright guitars, delighted with everything.

At the curb in front of Delgado she took him in with one look, from the knot of Theo’s half-Windsor down to the safety pins at his cuffs, and said nothing at all, and pulled out. She has saved it for the Rincon.
“Ted dressed you,” she says.
“How do you know?”
“Only Ted ties a half-Windsor on a Thursday.”

She’s in green herself, a dark knit dress with long sleeves and very little skirt, a shade off the tie — close enough that anybody who sees the two of them together tonight will assume they planned it. He has been waiting since half past three for the explanation. She told him she would explain nothing, and so far she is a woman of her word.

Past Ventura she thumbs the iPod off and the radio on, for the traffic, and gets the news instead: Salinger, dead at ninety-one in New Hampshire, the family announcing it today. Jack heard it at lunch, from Margot, with footnotes. Skye turns the man on the radio down to a murmur.

“Three agents,” she says. “Three auditions. Three different agents told me to read that book for three different sad-girl parts, like it was a vitamin. So I read it three times.” She checks her mirror and goes around a cement truck. “I hated him every time. He’s the only boy in literature who gets to hate everybody and still be the nice one.”
“He doesn’t hate everybody.”
“Name somebody.”
“Phoebe.”
“His little sister. She’s a sidekick. She’s there so he has somebody to be adorable at.”
“The ducks.”
“Everybody loves ducks.” She takes a hand off the wheel to wave all ducks away. “Ducks are the cheapest laugh in the business. Put a duck in a scene and I don’t care how bad the scene is.”

“His brother died,” Jack says. “Allie. Leukemia. The night it happened Holden slept in the garage and broke every window in it with his fist. He was thirteen. His hand still hurts when it rains.” The Santa Clara goes by under the bridge, wide and running brown after last week’s storms, the willows along it standing in the water to their knees. “You don’t do that because you hate everybody.”
She drives. Her thumb taps the wheel, not to anything on the radio. She reaches over and turns the radio the rest of the way off.
“Fine,” she says. “He’s grieving. He’s still the worst.” She puts the blinker on for Las Posas. “If he’d had you in the car he’d have been explained to himself by Camarillo.”
At the light at the bottom of the ramp she picks the white iPhone up off her lap and reads Corinne off it in Corinne’s vowels, every one of them ironed.
“*Arrive seven. Photographer at the valet. One hour. Civic.*” She says *civic* again, slower, like the name of a perfume. “She bills by the word.”
“Whose house?”
“Gil Abernathy’s. He runs the TV side of Meridian. He cries at his own pilots.” The light changes, and she drops the phone in the door pocket.

body.text: “And you owe me four minutes,” she says. “Like Studio City. Four minutes where nobody’s looking at me. I’m cashing them in a room full of donors.”
body.else: “You stand on my left,” she says, “half a step back. Like you’re carrying my bag and you’re proud of it.” He asks what’s in the bag. “Everything,” she says. “Act like it.”

body: Las Posas runs out through the strawberry fields to the sea, and PCH comes down along the Navy’s fence to Point Mugu, where the road goes through a notch somebody blasted out of the mountain years ago and leaves the big rock standing on the ocean side, out in the surf, with the last of the light going off the water behind it. After that it’s Malibu in the blue dark — lamps on in the houses on the sand, the water a paler black than the hills — and then the first lights coming on up in the canyons.
He tells her about the three honest knots.
“Ted has three honest knots and eleven coats. I’ve seen the closet.” She shakes her head at the road. “They’re all still auditioning.”
At a light by the pier she reaches over and moves his knot a hair to the left, and looks at it, and moves it back.

It’s full dark by the light at Sunset. The ocean is off to the right, heard more than seen, and on the near corner there’s a kiosk that used to belong to a gas station, the pumps long gone and the islands painted over, with a hand-lettered menu in the window and a heat lamp already on over two stools outside. The lamp makes a little orange room in the dark, about the size of a parking space, empty yet.

Skye has both hands at the top of the wheel, and her lips are moving. He doesn’t have to hear it; he knows the shape of it by now, Nonna’s prayer in Skye’s California — *since I can’t right now*, *as if You were already there* — said under her breath to a red light on the Pacific Coast Highway, and he watches her mouth do it and wants to marry the red light.

It goes green. She swings left, up Sunset, and the heat lamp slides away behind them in the mirror, and the road starts to climb into the hills, the houses stepping back from it behind hedges and gates. A block up, late, she finishes.
“Amen,” she says.
“Amen,” Jack says.

s03.slug: THURSDAY · 7:05 PM · THE PALISADES — A HOUSE ABOVE THE VILLAGE
body: The photographer is a heavy man in a fleece vest at the foot of the front steps, with a flash the size of a lunch box, and he gets them coming up out of the motor court: Skye’s hand through Jack’s arm, her face turned up to him, lit at nothing, and Jack in a borrowed suit, looking like a man in a borrowed suit, because he is. The flash leaves a pale blot floating on everything for the next twenty feet.
Corinne is just inside, at the near end of the bar, with her BlackBerry and a Diet Coke in a highball glass. She doesn’t look up. “Seven-oh-two,” she says, and types it.

The house is glass on three sides. To the east the city lies lit to the edge of the world, Santa Monica and Westwood and the towers downtown and the grid going on past them into a brown glow at the bottom of the sky. To the west there’s nothing at all, a black the windows give the room back in — every lamp twice, every guest twice — and somewhere down in it, the ocean.

Over the stairs to the lower floor somebody has hung a long blue banner with a senator’s name on it in white, and *2010*. On every tray that comes by, under the crab cakes and the little paper cones of tuna, there’s a cream card with a number to call and boxes to tick — $250, $1,000, $2,400, the most the law lets one person give. It’s an early fundraiser for Barbara Boxer, who is running for a fourth term. She isn’t here. It’s January, and a Thursday, and this is the kind of room a candidate comes to in October.
Jack takes a card off a tray, reads it, and puts it back where it was.

Gil Abernathy is a big, soft-spoken man with a tan he keeps up like a lawn. He calls Skye *kiddo* and holds her out at arm’s length to look at her, and shakes Jack’s hand with both of his, and says any friend of hers. His wife Janine has a silver bob and a real handshake, and asks Jack where he’s from, and when he says Youngstown she says, “Oh, *Ohio*,” warmly, and asks if it’s snowing there now.

Early on, a showrunner named Nate Shulman stands two steps up the staircase under the banner with a glass of red and says a few words. His show is about two detectives and a dog, and the dog tested best. “She’s running for a fourth term,” he says, “and I would like her to get it. I would also like *Harbor Division* to get a fourth season, and only one of those is up to the people in this room.” He finds the host with his glass. “Gil. I’m looking at you.” Gil roars loudest, and the room follows him, and Nate comes down off the stairs to a scatter of applause, pleased and a little embarrassed.

Skye works the room, and she is wonderful at it. She has the bartender’s name by her second club soda — he’s an actor too, a callback Tuesday for a cereal — and asks after the callback by her third. She gets Gil to tell the one about the network chairman and the koi pond. She remembers Janine’s daughter’s name, and the name of Janine’s daughter’s horse. Jack stands at her elbow and loves watching her be good at a thing. He counts the laughs as they go by: the big one for Gil is the job, and the ones for the donors are the job, and the one that gets out of her when the bartender does his cereal line for her, deadpan, with a bar spoon, isn’t.
A woman from the network takes her off his arm for a minute, and Jack ends up beside the shrimp.

Marla Kessler finds him there. She’s sixty or close to it, and she tells him in the first minute that she’s married to one of Nate’s writers and that before that she did legal aid in Fresno. She talks to him the way everyone in this house is going to talk to him all night, like a man who came in on Skye’s arm and so must be on her side of it.

“The Stupak people,” she says. “They passed it on a Saturday night in November and went home and slept fine. You know who doesn’t sleep fine? A girl waiting tables in Fresno with no insurance and no car and a bad month. I had clients like her for eleven years.” She looks at her wine. “I had a friend like her before that. She was nineteen. It was before. She didn’t go to a doctor, because there wasn’t one to go to.” She drinks. “So you’ll forgive me if I don’t find the man *principled*.”
Jack nods. He has an answer, and her friend is in it too. He eats the shrimp instead.

Glenn Sato produces something with helicopters in it. He comes by with a crab cake on a cocktail napkin and picks up where Marla left off. “Here’s what kills me,” he says. “Sixty is gone. Massachusetts took it. And the whole bill — thirty million people who can’t see a doctor — is hostage to the bishops. A handful of men in red hats, holding thirty million people over one line.” It’s a good line, and it comes out sounding like it’s been said before, somewhere with better light.
“Most of them wear purple, technically,” Jack says. “The red’s for cardinals.”

It doesn’t land. Glenn looks at him with honest puzzlement, and Jack takes a sip of his club soda, and Glenn goes back to his crab cake. By the windows a man is telling a woman that Bernanke got his seventy, thank God, and the woman says thank God is a strong word.
Five days ago he walked Market Street and the Embarcadero behind a banner, in sneakers. He can feel it in his shoes.

Waiters come through with trays of champagne, and somebody puts a flute in Jack’s hand. Gil goes up three steps under the banner and taps his glass with his wedding ring, and the room turns toward him, and the room in the black windows turns too. Across it, by the bar, Skye has a glass up already, saying something to the bartender that makes him put down the bar spoon.
Gil keeps it short. He raises his glass.
“To a woman’s right to choose,” he says, “and the votes to protect it.”
Every glass in the room goes up, and every glass in the windows goes up with it.

choices.text: *Hold it at your side.*
response: He doesn’t raise it. The champagne stays down by his pocket, going quietly flat, while the room drinks.

A waiter with an empty tray notices — a glance at the glass, a glance at him — and moves on. No one else does. Jack puts the polite face back on, the one for funerals and other people’s parishes, and wears it.

choices.text: *Raise it halfway. Don’t drink.*
response: The glass goes up as far as his shoulder and comes back down full. Across the room Janine Abernathy catches his eye over the rim of hers and smiles at him, and he smiles back.
It costs nothing, and it isn’t free. He keeps the polite face on and sets the full flute on a passing tray, carefully, so it won’t spill.

choices.text: *Find something urgent to do with a shrimp.*
response: For the length of the toast he is extremely interested in cocktail sauce. He dips. He weighs the depth of the dip. He dips again, with real care, the flute parked on the tablecloth beside the ice.
Glenn Sato catches him at it and raises his eyebrows at him, one comedian to another, as if it’s a bit. Jack lets him think so, and keeps the polite face on, with sauce on his thumb.

s04.slug: THURSDAY · 7:30 PM · THE PALISADES — THE TERRACE
body: The terrace runs the length of the west side, and it’s cold out here, January cold, the hills giving their day back to the sky. Two tall propane heaters hiss at either end over empty chairs. Jack stands at the rail and looks out at where the ocean is. He can’t see it. He can see Sunset winding down toward it in a string of streetlights, and the place where the lights stop.

He isn’t angry with her. He checks, like a man patting his pockets for his keys, and it isn’t there. She never said what tonight was for, and he never asked, and he’s nearly sure it never crossed her mind that anybody would need telling; in every room she has ever worked, nobody would. Pop would have walked out at the banner. Pop would have eaten the shrimp first. Jack has done neither, and somewhere around the toast he worked out that he isn’t going to, well before he worked out why.

She must have seen it from across the room; she reads a room the way he reads a book. The glass door slides behind him, and her heels come across the stone, and she’s at the rail beside him with her club soda.

body.text: “You raised your glass halfway,” she says. “I’ve never seen anybody look so Catholic holding a drink.”
“You’ve been holding that shrimp for six minutes,” she says. “It’s dead, Youngstown. Let it go.”
“You didn’t drink to it,” she says. “I watched you not.”

body: She bumps him with her hip. “What’s up, Youngstown? You’re doing your polite face.” She tips her head at him, smiling. “You’ve only got the one.”
“Nothing,” he says. “It’s a nice house.” He nods at the dark, the lights, the heaters. “Gil says you can see Catalina from the guest bathroom. He told me twice.”
She puts her glass down on the rail. She takes the cuff of his sleeve — Theo’s sleeve — between her finger and thumb, and keeps it.
“Jack,” she says. “What’s up?”

choices.text: “It’s a Boxer fundraiser, Skye. And it’s fine.”
choices.key: At the fundraiser Skye saw your face and asked twice. You told her what the room was for — and that it was fine, because she came to yours.
response: She turns and looks back through the glass at the banner, the cream cards going round on the trays, Gil coming down off the stairs with his flute, and he watches her read the room for the first time tonight, like a script on the second read, for what it’s actually about.
“Oh,” she says. “Oh, *Jack*. I didn’t even —” She has his cuff in her fist. “We’ll go. I’ll say I have a call time. I have a call time every night of my life, nobody will —”

“Skye. It’s fine.” He means the rest to come out light, and it doesn’t. “Saturday you drove six hours to walk a march for something you don’t believe in. You asked questions the whole way down Market Street, real ones, and you listened to the answers. You took us seriously. I can stand in a room for an hour and take them seriously back.”

She opens her mouth, and there’s nothing in it. She looks away from him, out at the city lit to the edge of the world, and her hand stays closed on his cuff, hard enough that he can feel her knuckles through Theo’s shirt.

choices.text: “Five days ago you walked my march, curious the whole way. I can stand in your room.”
choices.key: At the fundraiser Skye saw your face and asked twice. You told her she walked your march curious, so you could stand in her room.
response: She looks past him through the glass at the banner, the cards, the glasses that went up, and he can see her read it all at once and understand what he’s been standing in for half an hour.

“It’s for Boxer,” he says, so she doesn’t have to. “You didn’t think about it. Why would you. Saturday you didn’t believe a word on any of those signs, and you walked the whole thing anyway and argued with me fair, and didn’t make fun of it one time. So I can do this. I want to.”

She doesn’t say anything. She takes his arm the way she took it on the Embarcadero, high up, with both hands, and leans her weight into it, and for a little while she keeps her face turned against Theo’s shoulder where he can’t see it.

choices.text: “The shrimp and I have an understanding.”
choices.key: At the fundraiser Skye saw your face and asked twice. You made a joke about the shrimp — then told her what the room was for, and that it was fine.
response: Her head goes back, out over the hills, and she keeps hold of his sleeve, and raises her eyebrows at him: *and?*

So he gives her the real one anyway. “It’s a Boxer fundraiser. Every card on every tray.” She stops laughing. “And it’s fine. You came to mine. Six hours in the car, the whole of Market Street arguing, and you took every one of us seriously. I can do an hour in Gil’s.”
She reaches up and moves his knot a hair to the left, as she did at the light by the pier, and this time she doesn’t move it back. She leaves her hand there on Theo’s tie and looks at him over it.

s04a.slug: THURSDAY · 7:40 PM · THE PALISADES — THE FOOT OF THE STAIRS
body: When her head comes up, it’s to look through the glass at the near end of the bar, where Corinne stands with her Diet Coke and her BlackBerry, typing.

“Corinne,” Skye says. “It’s the march. Monday somebody two floors up asked her if Cassidy’s pro-life now, and tonight she put me under a Boxer banner, on your arm, with a man in a fleece vest at the foot of the steps.” She says it with something close to admiration. “She’s correcting San Francisco. And she needed you in the picture, or it doesn’t correct anything.”
“He got us at seven-oh-five.”

“He got us.” She turns her back on the city and leans on the rail and looks in at the room as he has seen her look at a set from the edge of it, counting the marks. “Okay. You’re staying for me. So here’s what I’m doing for you.”

She points with her chin, one at a time, through the glass. “Glenn’s red hats is a line. I heard him do it at a Christmas party, same order, same pause. Marla’s got a real one, and so does Nate, and Janine asks the question nobody wants at dinner and then pours you more wine.” She picks up her glass. “Half of that room has never been in a room with one of you who wasn’t on a sign or on cable. They’ve been arguing with a cartoon for thirty years and winning, and it’s made them lazy. They’re doing lines, Jack. I do lines for a living. I can hear it.”
“So what do you want?”

“I want you to give them the real ones. Your arguments, not the guy on the sign’s. In Gil’s living room, out loud, with me on the stairs.” She finishes the club soda. “You’ve been dying to since Marla said *principled*. I watched you eat your answer.”

She takes him back in on her arm, through the warm and the noise and the lamps doubled in the black glass, and at the foot of the stairs, under the long blue banner, she catches Gil by the sleeve and goes up one step, so that she’s a little above the room, and the room turns, the way it does when she talks.

“Gil. Everybody. This is Jack.” She has her hand on his shoulder. “On Saturday Jack walked the Walk for Life in San Francisco. I walked it with him, in sneakers, and argued with him for three miles, and I’m still voting for Barbara, so nobody panic.” The laugh comes up warm, just as she built it to. “He’s the only pro-lifer most of you are going to meet this year who isn’t on television. He’s very polite. He’s been eating shrimp all night so he wouldn’t say anything, and I think that’s a waste of a perfectly good Catholic.” She takes her hand back. “So ask him. Anything you want. Glenn, you go first. You’ve got the red hats ready.”
Gil roars, as he did for Nate, and throws up both his hands. “Kiddo. In my *house*?”
“You said any friend of mine.”

At the near end of the bar Corinne has stopped typing. Jack stands at the foot of a stranger’s stairs in a suit pinned up with Priya’s safety pins, under a banner for a senator his father would cross the street to avoid, with forty people turning toward him holding champagne, and it is the best he has felt in a room since he walked into this one.

s05.slug: THURSDAY · 7:50 PM · THE PALISADES — THE LIVING ROOM
body: Glenn Sato comes forward with a fresh crab cake and the good-sport face of a man who has been volunteered at a roast. “Okay,” he says. “Okay. I’ll go.” He counts them off on the hand with the napkin in it. “It’s a clump of cells. It’s her body, her choice. And if you don’t like abortion, don’t have one.” Here and there around the room heads nod along, a little early, the way people come in on the parts of a hymn they know.
“That’s three,” Skye says from the stair. “He’s pitching.”
“And the bishops —”
“We did the bishops.”
“They’re purple, apparently.” Glenn toasts Jack with the crab cake, and the room obliges, and Glenn looks pleased. “Go.”

Every face in the glass room comes around to Jack, and every face in the black windows comes with it. Janine Abernathy settles on the arm of a sofa with her glass. Nate Shulman leans on the newel post. Marla Kessler stays where she is, at the bar, and doesn’t smile, and watches him.

choices.text: “It isn’t a clump. Every embryology textbook says a new human organism starts at fertilization. That’s not the bishops. That’s chapter two.”
response: “Kevin Tran down the hall from me has Moore’s *The Developing Human* on his desk — it’s what they teach the pre-meds out of — and he’ll show it to anybody who stands still. Its own DNA the first day. A heartbeat by about six weeks. You don’t have to believe in anything to read it.” The room has gone quiet in the particular way of people who were expecting a pamphlet. “So the question was never when a human life starts, Glenn. The books settled that. The question is whether every one of them counts. That’s the only argument there is, and it’s a real one, and I’d rather have it with you than with a bumper sticker.”
Glenn opens his mouth on *cells* and shuts it, and points the crab cake up at Skye. “You said he was polite.”
“That was polite,” Skye says. “He answered you. Now you answer him back, Glenn. It’s improv. You have to say *yes, and*.”

choices.text: “‘If you don’t like abortion, don’t have one.’ Glenn, I’m doing my best.”
response: It gets the laugh, a big one, Gil’s on top of it. Jack waits it out and then gives them the rest.

“But listen to the sentence. If it’s a person in there, it doesn’t work — nobody says *if you don’t like it, don’t do it* about a thing that hurts somebody else. And if it isn’t a person, you don’t need the sentence at all. So all three of yours come back to one question: is it one of us. That’s the whole fight. Everything else is parking.”
Janine gets *parking* before anybody else does. Glenn looks at his three fingers, still up, and puts them down one at a time, like library books going back.

choices.text: “You’re right about the bishops. A handful of men in a room, and none of them carries anything.”
response: Glenn blinks. “Thank you?”

“It doesn’t change what’s in her. But I’m not going to stand in Gil’s living room and tell you a room full of men who’ll never be pregnant is the best messenger for this. My grandmother would tell you the same thing, and she lights candles for every one of them.”
“I’d like to meet your grandmother,” Glenn says, and seems to mean it.
“She’d pray for you at the TV,” Jack says, and Skye, on the stair, nods at Glenn gravely: *it’s true, she would*.

choices.text: “Leave the bishops out of it. Nat Hentoff is an atheist from the *Village Voice*, and he’s on my side of this.”
response: “He got there from the Bill of Rights,” Jack says. “Not from a catechism. You can get where I am without any God at all. It isn’t about who’s in charge of the Church. It’s about who counts.”
“Hentoff,” Glenn says. “The jazz guy?”
“The jazz guy.”

“Nat Hentoff wrote the notes on my first Mingus record,” Gil announces to the room, in wonder, as if Jack had produced a mutual friend, and from that moment on Gil is enjoying himself more than anybody in the house.

s05a.slug: THURSDAY · 8:20 PM · THE PALISADES — THE BAR
body: By the second round of crab cakes there are people sitting on Gil’s stairs. A man in a cashmere sweater has pulled up an ottoman. The bartender, who has a callback Tuesday for a cereal, has stopped pretending to polish anything.
“Marla,” Skye says from her step. “Tell him about your friend. He had an answer at the shrimp and he ate it.”
Marla Kessler comes down the bar with her wine and stops in front of him, close, and tells it to him and nobody else, though everybody hears.

“Her name was Lolly. Dolores. Nineteen, Fresno, nineteen seventy-one. She went to a man her cousin knew, and when it went bad she was afraid to go to a hospital and say why, so she didn’t. Four days.” She doesn’t look at her glass this time. “You want it illegal again. Fine. It won’t stop. It’ll go back to the cousins, and the girls who die will be the poor ones, and the girls who don’t will be poorer. Then you’ll go home to Ohio feeling clean.” She tilts her head. “What do you do for them on Monday, Jack? Not in heaven. Monday.”
The room doesn’t say anything. It’s her point, and everybody in Gil’s living room knows it, and so does he.

choices.text: “Then I owe her more than a law. A doctor, rent, a crib. Pass all of it, and I’ll march for that too.”
response: “With whose votes?” Marla says.
“Mine. Stupak’s. The ones you all keep calling hostage-takers. Give us the girl and the kid in the same bill and see who votes against it.”
“And until then?”

He has an answer for that, and she has one for his, and they go around it twice with the room turning its heads after them like a tennis crowd, and neither of them will call it, and Skye won’t call it for them.

choices.text: “I’m sorry about Lolly. She should never have been afraid of a hospital.”
response: Marla looks at him for a long time. “That’s the first time anybody on your side has said her name back to me.”
“I’d have walked for both of them.”
“You’d have walked *against* her.”
“For both of them,” Jack says. “Same walk.”
She sets her glass down on the bar. “Well, damn,” she says, to the glass, and the man on the ottoman snorts into his drink.

choices.text: “My mother’s parish has a closet in the basement full of cribs and car seats, and she has the key. That’s the part of us nobody films.”
response: He gives them the closet: the cribs stacked to the pipes, the car seats with the tags still on, the list taped inside the door of women from the parish who’ll drive you to a doctor at six in the morning and not ask your business. Ma’s key on the ring with the school keys and the church office.
“One closet,” Marla says.
“There’s one in every parish in Youngstown. It isn’t enough. It’s what there is while you and I argue.”
Marla looks at him over her wine. “Legal aid had a closet,” she says. “Third floor. Diapers.” And for a moment the two of them are standing in the same closet, and they both know it.

choices.text: “You did legal aid for eleven years for girls nobody else would help. You’re more pro-life than half my parish, and you’re going to hate that I said it.”
response: She does hate it. It’s all over her face, and then the laugh comes up through it anyway, short and appalled.
“Don’t you dare,” she says.
“I’m Catholic. I dare all the time. We have a sacrament for it.”
She takes a card out of her evening bag and tucks it into Theo’s breast pocket, where Theo forbade a pocket square. “Fresno,” she says. “Come see my old office. Then dare.”

s05b.slug: THURSDAY · 8:50 PM · THE PALISADES — THE STAIRS
body: Nate Shulman has come down off the newel post and sat on Gil’s stairs two below Skye, his red wine on his knee. “Philosophy major?” he says.
“Yes.”

“Then you know the violinist.” He says it for the room, though, settling in, a man who has pitched in better rooms than this and enjoyed every one. “Judith Jarvis Thomson, nineteen seventy-one. You wake up in a hospital bed. A society of music lovers has kidnapped you in the night and plugged your kidneys into a famous violinist who’ll die without them, and the doctor says: nine months, and then he’s fine. Grant it all. Grant he’s a person, with every right to life a person has.” He opens his free hand. “Nobody can make you stay plugged in. A right to life isn’t a right to the use of somebody else’s body. That’s the argument. Thomson gives you the person, and still wins.”
It’s the best thing anybody has said all night, and Nate knows it, and he doesn’t make anything of knowing it.
“Do the violinist, Jack,” Skye says. “He did it for me on Market Street, and his was better than mine.”

Corinne has come down the room with her BlackBerry lit in her palm, and she stops at the foot of the stair and holds it up for Skye to see. “Your mother,” she says, in the vowels, “would like to know if it’s a scene.”
“Tell her it’s a hit,” Skye says.
Corinne types it. She doesn’t go back to the bar afterward. She stays where she is, with one hand on Gil’s banister, watching Jack as she watched him at lunch, but without the pad.

choices.text: “Unplugging the violinist lets him die of what he already had. An abortion doesn’t unplug anybody. It ends somebody. Those are two different acts.”
response: “Tell that to the woman,” Nate says, “for whom it’s the same nine months.”
“I would. I’d tell her I know it’s the same nine months. And it’s still a different act. One’s letting go. The other one’s doing something to somebody.”
Nate tips his glass at him and then at Skye, a point given and a point kept in one gesture, and the room can’t tell whose it is, and neither can Jack.

“And the father?” Nate says. “In your Fresno. Where’s his coat?”
“He owes it too. More. That’s the part my side’s worst at, and you’re right to hit us with it.”
Nate takes a cocktail napkin off the stair and writes something on it with the bartender’s pen, and folds it, and puts it in his jacket.

“I still think the kid didn’t choose any of it either. I still think he counts. But it’s the hardest thing anybody ever asks anybody. It ought to be hard to say.”
Over at the bar Marla has turned all the way around on her stool. On the stair above Nate, Skye has her chin in her hand and has stopped doing anything at all but listening.

response: “It tested well,” Nate says, at once, and the room comes apart, and Gil has to put his glass down.

When it’s back Jack gives him the real answer, shorter than he would have on Market Street: that walking away from the violinist lets him die of what he already had, and an abortion doesn’t walk away from anybody; and that the violinist is a stranger, and a kid is your own.
“Order it to series,” Skye tells Gil, and Gil, delighted, says he’ll take it to the network.

s05c.slug: THURSDAY · 9:20 PM · THE PALISADES — THE WINDOWS
body: Janine Abernathy waits until the room has settled. Then she gets up off the arm of the sofa with her glass and comes over to stand with Jack by the black windows, where the two of them stand twice, and says it to his reflection as much as to him.
“I have one,” she says. “You marched for life. Are you for the death penalty?”
“Mostly,” Jack says.

“Then it isn’t life you’re for. It’s innocence.” She says it warmly, a hostess offering the last of something. “Which is fine. It’s a position. But if it’s innocence, honey, you had better be for that health bill top to bottom, because the innocent get born on Medi-Cal. And you had better be on the side of that girl the day after the baby comes, and the year after, and not just the nine months before. My husband’s network has made eleven seasons of television about people who are consistent right up until it costs them.” She touches his glass with hers. “That’s my question.”
Across the room Gil raises his hands in surrender, proud of her. On the stairs Skye says nothing; she’s watching Jack, not Janine, to see what he’ll do with it.

choices.text: “It’s innocence, yes. The man on death row did something. The kid in Fresno hasn’t done anything but exist.”
response: “And you’re sure about every man on death row?” Janine says.

He isn’t, and he says so. Ohio has let men out of its prisons with DNA tests in their hands; he’s read about them in the *Vindicator*, men from towns he could drive to. Janine nods, and doesn’t press it, and doesn’t need to. It’s her point, and he takes it from her and holds on to it.

choices.text: “You got me. My own Church says the cases where you need it are practically nonexistent, and I keep arguing with my own Church. I should probably quit.”
response: “John Paul said it in ’95,” he tells her. “*Evangelium Vitae*. If there’s any other way to protect people, you use it. My sister’s religion teacher has it on a poster, and I’ve been walking past the poster since I was twelve.”
Janine is delighted. “A man,” she tells the room, “who loses a point in my living room. Gil. Write it down.”
At the foot of the stairs Corinne, who has no pad, takes out her BlackBerry and writes something down.

choices.text: “Then hold me to all of it. I’m for most of that bill — every part that pays for her and the kid. I’m against the part that pays to end it. That’s one line. I’ll walk it.”
response: “You don’t get dropped for getting sick. You don’t get turned down for what you’ve already got. Her prenatal, his shots, her teeth.” He holds up one finger. “Not the abortions. You want me consistent, that’s me consistent, and I’ll take the hit from both of your parties for it.”
“And the war?” Janine says.
“Ask me about Iraq some night when your husband isn’t paying for the bar.”
She clinks his glass again, and goes to tell Gil she likes him.

choices.text: “Consistency’s a good thing to ask about in a house this size. Is the woman who cleans it on Gil’s insurance?”
response: It lands. The room hears it land; somebody’s ice is very loud.

Gil, across the room, doesn’t get red. He answers it as if somebody had called roll. “Rosa,” he says. “Rosa Echeverría. Since two thousand four. And her daughter, since last spring.” He says it to Jack without any heat at all, and that’s worse than heat would have been.

And then Skye is down off the stair and has Jack’s arm, laughing, easy, carrying the whole room back up with her as she comes. “That’s *my* line,” she tells them. “I did it in the car on the way down, about somebody else’s house, and now he’s doing it in Gil’s, which is rude, Jack. And Gil *passed*.” Gil gives a great bark of delight, and the room comes back with him, relieved, and the ice goes back to being ice.
With her mouth an inch from his ear, still smiling at everybody, she says, “Don’t do it twice.”

s05d.slug: THURSDAY · 10:05 PM · THE PALISADES — THE MOTOR COURT
body: The party should have ended at nine. It ends at ten, because nobody wants to go first, and Gil walks them to the door himself with an arm around each of them.

body.text: On the top step he keeps Jack’s hand in both of his. “Kiddo,” he tells Skye, “he *won*. Don’t tell Barbara.”
“He won Glenn,” Skye says. “Marla won Fresno, Janine won Ohio, and I won the room.” She ticks them off on Theo’s lapel, and Jack wouldn’t argue a single one.

Marla Kessler catches them on the top step with her coat on and stops Jack with a hand on Theo’s lapel. “You argue like a man who’d rather keep the friend than the point,” she says. “It’s very annoying. Come to Fresno.”
“He does that,” Skye says. “I’ve been trying to break him of it since Thanksgiving.”

Nate Shulman stops them on the top step and declares the evening a draw, pending a rewrite, and shakes Jack’s hand on it, formally, with Gil holding his wine for him as a witness. Skye asks for it in writing. Nate says it’s Hollywood; nothing’s in writing.

body: From the doorway behind them Glenn Sato shouts, “You’re wrong! That was the best time I’ve had at one of these since Dukakis!” and Janine pulls him back inside by the sleeve.

Corinne is at the foot of the steps in her coat, with the BlackBerry put away for the first time all night. She looks Jack up and down, the borrowed suit, the pins, the crab-cake crumbs on Theo’s lapel.
“You were supposed to be furniture,” she says. Then, to Skye: “Post the arrival picture tonight. It’s on the wire already. It needs you under it.”
“Goodnight, Corinne,” Skye says, sweetly, and Corinne goes off down the motor court toward a black Audi without saying it back.

The valet brings the Saab around with its top up and its bumper still dented, and holds her door, and she doesn’t get in. She stands by it in the white light of the motor court in the green dress and looks at Jack across the roof.
“People walk out of rooms for me all the time,” she says. “Agents. Boyfriends. My mother, every Christmas.” Her hand is spread on the roof of the car. “You’re the first one who ever stayed in one.”

response: He doesn’t say anything to that. He comes around the car and kisses her, and walks her back with it until the Saab is behind her.

She makes a sound against his mouth, half a laugh, and her hands come up inside his collar, cold from the terrace, and his hands are on the car roof on either side of her, the metal ice under his palms, and he wants her hips in them instead, and the green dress gone, and the long dark drive and all night after it — he wants more than kissing, and he wants it all through him.
Somewhere behind them the valet coughs. Skye, without stopping, takes one hand off the back of Jack’s neck and waves at him.

choices.text: “I’d do it again. Every room.”
choices.key: In Gil Abernathy’s motor court Skye said you’re the first person who ever stayed in a room for her. You told her you’d do it again, every room.
response: She has Theo’s tie in her hand before he’s done saying it, and pulls him around the bumper by it until the Saab is at his back, and kisses him.

The cold of the door comes through Theo’s shirt in a stripe across his shoulder blades. Her hips are against his, and he puts his hands on them, on the thin green knit and the warm of her under it, and he wants — the dress up, and the motor court gone, and her, now — and the wanting goes through him from his mouth to his knees, and he lets it.
When she lets go of the tie it’s wrecked. She looks at it in the white light and puts her forehead against his chin. “Ted’s going to kill you,” she says. “That was a *commitment*.”

choices.text: “I came for the shrimp.”

response: “The shrimp had it coming,” she says, and kisses him before she’s done laughing, so the start of it is mostly teeth.

She pulls him in by his belt against her, against the Saab’s cold flank, and his hands go to her hips and find the green knit and her under it, and he wants more than this — the dress up and the long road home and the rest of the night to spend somewhere with a door.
The valet, a kid from Santa Monica College with a chemistry textbook under his arm, finds something urgent to look at on the far side of the motor court.

s06.slug: THURSDAY · 10:40 PM · TACOS EL FARO, SUNSET AT PCH
body: The radio sits on a shelf over the flat-top, a paint-flecked Panasonic with a coat hanger for an antenna, playing something old and slow with strings in it, and the cook sings the chorus under her breath while she scrapes down the griddle. Every time she throws meat on, the flat-top goes up in a hiss and a cloud, and the cloud comes out the window and hangs under the heat lamp with them.

It’s the kiosk on the corner they passed at the red light three and a half hours ago, on the way up. Coming back down Sunset with the heater going and the hills dark on both sides, Skye said, “I ate one shrimp and a speech. I want real food,” and swung in under the lamp before the light changed. Out on the old pump island there are two plastic tables and four chairs that don’t match — two white, one green, one child-sized and red — and they have the lamp’s little orange room to themselves. Across the highway the surf is loud in the dark.

The cook’s name is Ofelia. It’s stitched over the pocket of her apron in red thread, under a red lighthouse to match the sign. When the two of them came across the lot out of the Saab — Skye in the green dress with her heels hooked on her fingers, Jack in a borrowed suit that has been argued in for two hours — Ofelia leaned out of her window and said, “Ay, *mija*. Where are your shoes,” and then, “Sit. Sit, sit,” and fed them.

Skye ordered for both of them in a Spanish she says she learned from grips — mostly meat and swearing — and asked for extra limes. Ofelia rang up fifty cents for the limes and held her hand out for it, and Skye paid in quarters, one at a time, onto the little steel counter in the window.

“She charged me for limes,” she said when she sat down, looking at her two quarters’ worth on the paper plate like they’d come out of a mine. “Do you know how long it’s been since anybody charged me for a lime?”

Since then there’s been a second round, and his Mexican Coke in the glass bottle, and her horchata going to slush, and the talk has gone everywhere Gil’s living room didn’t. Whether a hot dog is a taco: yes, she says, structurally; it’s a sandwich that won’t admit what it is, he says. Somewhere in the second round Ofelia came out with a paper boat of grilled onions and one charred jalapeño they didn’t order and set it in front of Jack. “*Para el flaco*,” she said. He has been called worse. He ate the jalapeño to be polite and has been crying on and off ever since.
Skye’s phone buzzes on the table by the limes. She reads it off the screen in Corinne’s vowels. “*Post the arrival. Tonight. It’s civic.*” She turns the phone face down on the paper plate.
“Post it,” Jack says. “It’s fine. You got photographed with me at the march. You can get photographed with me at Boxer’s. It’s only fair.”

Skye looks at him across the plastic table for a long moment, and takes a breath, and blows him a raspberry: long, wet and magnificent, the kind a person learns from a boom operator on a night shoot. Ofelia leans out of her window to see who’s dying.

“No,” Skye says. She points a lime at him. “A girl named Kenzie put me in a picture at your march without asking. I looked her up; she sings. She didn’t mean anything by it, and you saw tonight what it cost. So I’m not going to do on purpose to you what she did to me by accident.” She squeezes the lime in his general direction. “You didn’t come to Gil’s for Barbara. You came for me. I’m not putting you under her name.”

Kenzie Rourke: the cantor at the 9:30, Peter Haddad’s girlfriend, the front seat of the van on Saturday with a road atlas open to a page they’d left an hour back. He likes her fine and couldn’t tell you her major. He cracks up — at the raspberry, at Ofelia hanging out of her window, at the lime juice on Theo’s lapel — and Skye cracks up at him, and that’s when she does it: the white iPhone out low across the table at the end of her arm, the back of it to them, blind, over the horchata and the paper boats, and the two of them turned to each other and not to it. It makes its little shutter sound.

She brings it in and tips it to the heat lamp and looks at it, and starts typing with both thumbs, the tip of her tongue in the corner of her mouth, and won’t let him see until it’s up. Then she turns it around on the table so it faces him.

body.text: “About Rosa,” she says, with a lime in her fingers. “Gil’s housekeeper.”
“That was cheap.”
“It was good,” she says. “That’s the problem with you.” She squeezes the lime over a taco that has had plenty. “Don’t do it twice. Okay. Health care. Go.”

body: “You heard me tell Janine. Most of it, yes. Not the abortion money.” He steals one of her limes. “And I’m against it coming out of Washington, because nothing comes out of Washington without a string on it, and the other end of the string’s in the hand of somebody who’s never been to Ohio.”

“Sixty is gone,” she says. “The man with the truck took it.” She means the senator-elect’s pickup; it has been on every channel since. “So they pass the Senate’s, or they go home and explain to people why they didn’t. I’m for it. All of it, the strings too. Strings are how you hold something up.”
“Strings are how you work a puppet.”
“Your father’s union got him a doctor,” she says. “Whose union got Rudy one?”

It lands. Rudy at the flat-top at the Anchor in his hairnet, turning hash browns — Jack has worked that counter beside him since the fall and couldn’t tell you the name of his doctor, or if there is one. “Rudy’s tooth,” Skye says, and touches her own jaw, low on the left. “The night Gloria gave me the boysenberry. He chewed on the other side all night.” Jack goes back through that night and can’t find the tooth anywhere in it. So he gives her the true thing instead, the one he doesn’t tell people: since Lordstown the Costigans are on Ma’s insurance, the diocese’s plan, and Pop carries the card behind his union card, where he doesn’t have to look at it.

It’s a game with her, and they both know it: she argues to win, and she argues to find out, and he can tell which by whether she stops on his answer and turns it over before she knocks it down. Two people who are never going to agree about Washington, playing for keeps over a paper boat of onions, and having the time of their lives.
“The bailout,” she says. “Let’s do one you’re wrong about.”

“I’m for it. GM goes under, Lordstown goes with it, and every bar and diner and parish for twenty miles goes with Lordstown. It didn’t save my dad; they took his shift in June. It saved the plant. They still build the Cobalt out there.” He looks around the empty lot. “There isn’t one in this zip code.”

“So the men who run GM fly to Washington in their own jets to ask for money, and get a bridge loan by Christmas. And the year before that the writers go out for three months, and every show in this town goes dark, and nobody bridges anybody anything.” She holds up the lime like a vote. “I’m a union member, Jack. Two of them. SAG and AFTRA. I paid dues before I could drive.”
“Half the Valley eats off Lordstown. Nobody eats off a sitcom.”
“Tell that to the juicers.”
“The what?”

“Juicers. Electricians. The grips do the flags, and they’ll fight you if you mix them up; the juicers do the light.” She squeezes the lime over nothing. “My father was a juicer. Pat Doyle. Meridian, mostly. Whatever stage was shooting, he was up over it on a ladder or out on the catwalk with a lamp the size of a trash can, and I was underneath in a car seat, I’m told. I don’t remember any of it.” She puts the lime down. “He left when I was four. Or he was made to. Depends which one of them you ask, and you can only ask one of them.”
“Your mother.”

“My mother took his name off everything. The mailbox. The bank. The hyphen.” She draws a short line in the air with her finger and rubs it out. “When I got my SAG card I was Skye Callender, and that was the first thing I ever signed. I practiced the *S* for a week.”
“What do you know about him?”

“He took his coffee with so much sugar the craft-service guy kept a separate jar for him, with *PAT* on it in tape. I got that from the craft-service guy.” She wipes her fingers on a napkin, one at a time. “He sent a card every birthday till I was nine, care of the studio. *Dad (Pat).* With the Pat in parentheses. Like I might need a footnote.”
“Did you ever see him again?”

“Once. I was fourteen. A pilot on Stage Nine — I was a girl who could hear dead people; it didn’t go. Between setups the gaffer leaned down to me and said, *Pat Doyle says hi*, and pointed up.” She points up, at the heat lamp. “There was a man on the catwalk with his hand up. Just up. Like a kid in class who knows the answer.” Her hand comes down to the table. “It’s a really big stage. Neither of us crossed it.”
“You wanted to,” Jack says.
“I was in a harness. For a stunt. I couldn’t have got up a ladder in it if I’d tried.” She laughs at herself, short. “That’s what I tell myself. The harness.”

Jack gets up and drags the green chair around the table, over the bolts where a pump used to stand, and sets it down against hers and sits, so that their shoulders touch and they’re both facing the same way, out at the highway and the dark where the water is. She leans into him. For a while it’s the surf and the radio and Ofelia singing over the scraper.

Then she picks her phone up off the table and thumbs past the picture, past Corinne, up through today — *outside*, *theo says 5 more min*, *im timing him* — to Wednesday night, and turns it so he can see. There it is, the last thing before Thursday: *nonna wants your baptism name. if you have one.*
“You never answered it,” he says.

“I never answered it.” She looks at it on the little screen. “I’ve read it about forty times. In the car. In Gil’s guest bathroom. It has a view of Catalina, I’m told.” She sets the phone down by the limes. “I didn’t text it back because I wanted to say it out loud the first time.”
Over in the window Ofelia has stopped scraping to listen to the radio. A truck goes north on PCH and its wind comes across the pump island and moves the paper plates.
“Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle,” Skye says, in her own voice.
Jack doesn’t move. She keeps going, quickly.

“St. Mary’s, in Lancaster. I was six weeks old. There’s one picture, and I look furious about it. His mother was Mary Catherine — the grandmother. I met her twice. She called me all of it, both times, every syllable, like it was a title I’d won.” She tears the paper off her straw in a slow spiral. “My mother lost that one. She’s told me so. It’s the only thing I’ve got she didn’t name.”
She picks the lime back up.
“Ted knows,” she says. “Ted’s always known. He’s never used it.”

body: The radio has gone to ads, a mattress store in Pico Rivera shouting about Presidents’ Day already, and Ofelia is wiping down the flat-top in long slow strokes, letting the grill go cold. “*Everything must go*,” Skye says, in the mattress man’s voice, right on his beat, and Ofelia says something to it in Spanish that the station would have to bleep. A minute ago Skye asked him to send it. “Your nonna,” she said. “Tonight. Before I talk myself out of it.” He typed it on the RAZR with his thumb, and stopped after the second name, and she saw him stop. “The rest is yours,” he told her. “You give her that part.”

body: “It’s ten to four there,” he says, the third time she asks him to check. “Gina’s asleep. Nonna’s asleep. The furnace is asleep.”
“She’ll pray it,” he says. “She’s been praying for you since Christmas. Now she’s got the right name to do it under.”

Skye takes the RAZR out of his hand and opens it and checks it herself. In the window Ofelia reaches up and switches off her sign, the red lighthouse and the word over it, and leaves the heat lamp burning for them a little longer.

He wakes because the road has started to bend, and the sea is right there. The Rincon: the 101 running north along the edge of the continent, a guardrail and a scatter of riprap and then the Pacific, black, with the surf coming in white in long lines under a moon a night short of full. The top is up. The heater is on low. There is nothing in the Saab but the tires and the water.

Skye is driving with her feet bare on the pedals and Theo’s suit jacket over her like a blanket, the sleeves hanging down either side of the seat. Somewhere since Malibu she has put her hair up with the rubber band off Ofelia’s to-go bag.
“You snore in Spanish now,” she says.
He sits up and scrubs his face with both hands. Up ahead the lights of Carpinteria are coming, a gas station lit white as an operating room, a sign for a motel with the *O* out.
“What’s your family going to say?” she says. “About the picture.”
She asks it easily, eyes on the road, but with her free hand she has pulled the jacket up to her chin.

He tells her the truth, because it’s the middle of the night on the Rincon and there isn’t anything else he’d want to tell her. “Gina’s going to scream, and then text me about it till chemistry. Ma’s going to say you’re beautiful. Pop’s going to grunt, which means you’re beautiful. Nonna’s going to say you’re beautiful and too thin, and ask what you eat, and not believe the answer.” The road bends, and the Saab leans into it, and comes out of it. “And then every one of them is going to ask me if you’re Catholic.”
He looks over at her, at her jaw in the green of the dash lights.
“Now I can say yes.”
Her right hand comes off the wheel and finds his knee in the dark, and grips it, and goes back to the wheel.

At the Delgado curb the building is dark except for the east stairwell, always lit, and the Saab idles. She kisses him across the gearshift, and again, and he gets a hand in her hair and the rubber band goes somewhere neither of them will ever find it, and she bites his lower lip, not hard, and kisses it better. Only kisses, slow ones, the windows fogging over around them.
At a quarter to three she puts her hand on his chest, open, and pushes him back into his own seat.
“You have class.”
“It’s Friday.”

“You have *Friday*.” She shrugs Theo’s jacket off her shoulders and hands it across to him. “Tell Ted it had a nice time.” She reaches over him and opens his door herself. “Go be smart. I’ll call you when I wake up, which will be noon, because I’m famous, unless Corinne gets to me first.”
He gets out, and the cold finds him through Theo’s shirt, and he goes up the Delgado steps with the jacket over his arm. Halfway up he turns around to go back down to the car.
The curb is empty.
He stands on the step a long time, wanting to have gone back.
