journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big. Friday the sun came out, and she called the telethon as Skylark. Saturday she drove six hours to the Walk for Life, walked the whole thing arguing with me, and stood in front of Clare when a man started screaming. Sunday she came to Mass. I told her why I didn’t go up. Out past the break I told her what I know about the basement, which isn’t much, and about Nonna’s question and Danny’s. She’s the answer to both. She knows there’s more; she said that’s enough. She asked me to teach her Nonna’s prayer. Monday a blog found the back of my head; Gina knew Danny’s jacket before the commenters did. Corinne called her at six: every picture of us down until there’s a strategy. At noon in her room I was the one who didn’t want to stop, and she stopped it — for Sunday. She’d read up on confession to do it: I can’t walk in on Wednesday with a plan, and she won’t be my plan. Ask her again after she’s watched me go up. She asked me what I lose when I sit in the pew, and I told her: they pass the plate over you. She watched them do it on Sunday and didn’t know what she was watching. Then she took a picture of us without looking, and that night she put it up, captioned with Corinne’s own rule — *my friend from school.* At the lunch in Studio City her shoes stayed on. When they got to Danny she came back for that and nothing else, and said his number from memory. In the car she said she’s very good at fine. She heard me tell Ma *tomorrow*, and that I think she’s the answer, and took the picture down at the Las Posas exit without a word. Sol’s swing is up. I told her I don’t care, and she could tell. She’s stopping anyway. She wants Nonna to like her. Wednesday she said Theo and Laney were running lines. Wednesday night she was at the curb when I got home from confession. She asked if I went. Then, in the middle of a bit about a Supreme Court justice, I said it first. I didn’t know I was going to. She’d been carrying it since Monday, and she was going to say it first. She said it back. Thursday she took me to a fundraiser in the Palisades and never said what for — it didn’t occur to her anybody would mind. It was for Boxer: Corinne wanted me in the picture so the march would stop being a story. She saw my face across the room and asked twice. I told her it was fine — she came to my Walk and took the other side seriously, so I could stand in hers. So she went back in and got the whole room to argue with me, the real arguments, in Gil’s living room, for two hours, and made sure every one of them knew where I stand. We stayed till the end. At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset she wouldn’t post Corinne’s picture. She blew me a raspberry and posted one of us at the table instead: we agree on each other, and we’re not just friends from school. She’s a union member. Two of them. Her father was Pat Doyle, a juicer on the Meridian lots, gone since she was four. Then she said her name. Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle. Baptized at St. Mary’s in Lancaster, named for his mother. The only name she has that her mother didn’t give her. I sent the first two to Gina for Nonna. At three in the morning I made the picture my profile picture. She says I stole her art. She says happy looks good on me.

s09.slug: FRIDAY · 1:15 PM · HOLLIS HALL, THE BACK STEPS
body: The back steps of Hollis face the loading dock and the afternoon sun, and a dumpster that somebody in Art has painted with a dolphin, so they are warm by one o’clock and hardly anyone uses them. Jack takes the second one down with a Commons banana and his bag between his feet, forty minutes before his two o’clock.
The RAZR goes against his thigh before he has the banana open. GINA, across the little outside screen.
“Okay,” Gina says. “I have the late bus in eight minutes and I’m doing it in order.”
Behind her a row of diesels idles in the Ursuline lot with the heaters on, and a salt truck scrapes by, and a trunk slams.
“Hi, Gina.”
“Hi. Number one. Nonna. She said it nine times at breakfast. I counted under the table on my fingers. Rosie says ten, but Rosie counts the one she said to the toast.”
“It’s Mary Catherine,” Jack says.

“Not on Glenwood it isn’t. She made it Italian without being asked. She held the phone out at arm’s length like she was at the eye doctor and read it off the screen and kept going. Good crying. There’s two kinds, I’m an expert. Then she wouldn’t touch her eggs till somebody drove her to church, so we all went, before the 8:00 school Mass, and she went up the side aisle to Our Lady and put her money in and lit a tall one. Ma said *Mamma, we’ll be late*, and Nonna said *La Madonna non è mai in ritardo*, which means —”
“The Madonna’s never late.”

“I got a tardy slip for it. It says *family devotion*. And she looked up which Catherine in her missal, and it’s Alexandria. The wheel one. She out-argued fifty professors and they tried to kill her on a wheel. Nonna says Rome took her off the calendar in nineteen sixty-nine and put her back in two thousand two and never said sorry.”
“Fifty,” Jack says. “Did she win all fifty?”
“Nonna said *brava*. To a saint. Like at a recital.”

He thinks of Skye at a red light on Thursday with Nonna’s prayer going under her breath, and of Nonna in the side aisle at St. Brigid’s with her money in her fist: two women who have never met, working the same Madonna from either end of the country. The banana is half peeled, and he has forgotten it.

“Number two. Ma. She went down to the Dell in her coat before work and looked at the picture for a full minute. I was on the stairs. It wasn’t the Tuesday face, I know the Tuesday face. She said something about her size. I’m not repeating it, she’ll say it to you herself, it’s hers. Then she read the writing under it out loud, all of it, the parenthesis too, and didn’t say anything. Then she clicked on your name and it was the same picture, and she said *Gina, it’s the same picture*, and I said *that’s the point, Ma*.”

body.text: “And Ryan Pallante texted me. Ryan has not texted me since the fifth grade. *My mother printed your brother’s yes and put it on the refrigerator under St. Joseph.* With the period in it, Jack. He’s mortified.”

body: “And everybody at school keeps asking is she Catholic, and does she pray, and is she nice in real life, and not one of them asked about —”
“Gina.”
He pulls the banana the rest of the way open.
“— the *weather*,” Gina says. “Out there. Jeez. I was going to say the weather.”
“Number three. Did you mail it?”
“This morning. The slot in the mailroom.”
“Then it’s late. It goes in with mine Monday, and then it sits in their mailroom while a CO reads your handwriting, so it’s *very* late. That’s fine. Late’s fine. Mine has a candle on it.”

“Number four. Sunday’s Ma’s Sunday and I’m coming. Ma said yes if my chemistry’s done by Saturday night, so it will be. I’m telling him the name. In person, across the table. He’s going to *lose it*.”
“Wait till he’s eaten something.”
“Obviously after. I’m not an animal.”
Behind her the air brakes let go, and the doors fold open on their long hydraulic sigh, and a driver somewhere calls *Let’s go, ladies*.
“Bus. That’s mine — I love you, that was on a bus, it doesn’t count.”
The doors thump shut on her end, and the RAZR goes back to being a phone.

journal.title: Gina
journal.text: My sister. Fifteen, a sophomore at Ursuline. Texts in lowercase like punctuation costs extra. A girl in religion class called her the class expert on visiting the imprisoned. Dad turned the radio back on. Nonna told the altar society I went to confession. Said Danny’s name back to the girl. The girl looked away first. Then laughed with Kelsey anyway. Gina wants the first part on the record. She wanted to know if the nun was real. Now they’re Facebook friends, and Lena signs her wall posts like letters. Gina found the boyfriend in about four minutes. Didn’t tell Nonna. Ashley Vrabel is going to Halloween as a prisoner. Orange jumpsuit. A tribute, she says. Lena read it once and gave me a line for her. Halloween: went as a nun, obviously. Ashley wore the jumpsuit. Gina said it — visit, not dress up as — and Kelsey laughed at Ashley for once. Ashley says she’s dead Monday. Ashley sat next to her in religion and didn’t say anything. Kelsey either. The radio says they’re firing the GM. Dad laughed, Ma says. First time since June. Tuesday she said the thing about Ashley Vrabel’s father in religion. Detention. She thought it would feel good. She heard Dad’s truck hit the can Monday night. Team Edward. Jacob is literally a dog. Monday she found Nonna at the bottom of the stairs, and called the ambulance, and went for Dad. Said sorry to Ashley. Told me in the next text. On the floor in Denver I asked her to look up a girl. She screamed. She’s sworn. ‘Not even the nun?’ Thanksgiving: met me at the door — on TV, in person. Took Danny’s call and said nothing. Printed the dock picture on Ma’s ink. Translated Nonna for Theo, mostly. Checked Facebook for me — Becca took it down. ‘You looked like you were doing a shift.’ Gave Ashley Vrabel the peace at the first candle. Still sworn. Christmas: kept it thirty days. Lifted a hand to Ashley Vrabel at the Orange Julius first, and Ashley lifted one back. Gave me the second season of *Sweetwater*, for research — and Rosie handed it to me in front of everybody. She meant upstairs. Put season two in the DVD player the day after Christmas, for research, and the whole family watched. Wrote Danny about the boat. It’s a yacht. Filmed everybody’s resolutions on Theo’s Flip. Found the baptism album before I did. “Who’s the guy?” At the door, in my ear: “Don’t let Ma find out from Facebook.” Tuesday: six thousand views; Ashley Vrabel showed the whole bus. Nonna lit a candle and won’t say for who. On my wall: FINALLY — the sister who knew first. Monday she found me on a celebrity blog before I did, and knew Danny’s jacket. A man from Mahoning County called Danny a name in the comments; she reported him, answered him, and called him one back — a Catholic one. She’s making Danny a card for Candlemas. Tuesday Ashley Vrabel showed her the picture in chem. Capitals. Wednesday, at three in the morning her time: Nonna wants a baptism name, for the rosary. Friday she was lowercase again: *mary catherine?????* Nonna said it nine times at breakfast and lit a candle for her at St. Brigid’s. My Candlemas card for Danny goes in her envelope Monday. Sunday’s Ma’s Sunday. She’s telling him in person.

journal.title: Nonna
journal.text: Asked me about the girl. Laughed. Five minutes later she asked me again, the same words, like it was the first time. Ma says she’s tired. That was the nineteenth of September. Michaelmas she lit one for me and one for Danny. Saturday: ‘E la ragazza?’ Ma told her the girl has a boyfriend. ‘Peccato.’ Then, sharp: ‘E l’altra?’ Purdue Saturday. Dad said ‘Purdue’ and that was the call. Nonna got on the extension and called me Danny. Then she knew me. Then she asked about the crab girl. Sunday the 8th: ‘E la ragazza?’ Which one, I didn’t ask. She didn’t say. Monday she fell on the stairs she’d been keeping off. St. Elizabeth’s: her wrist, six stitches, a monitor for her heart. Called the paramedic handsome. Dad drove her. Home Thanksgiving morning. Cast to the elbow; a monitor on her housedress. Kept both cards — the nun’s and the other one. Made Theo her hands. Sat him in the chair. Says she’ll pray for him, starting that night. Knows it isn’t the nun. Christmas: Mémère’s still lighting her whole name — “Carmela Rinaldi. Tutto.” Asked if Danny’s coming, more than once. Set his place at the Vigil, and Ma left it. Pointed at the girl on the DVD: *l’attrice*. Theo’s cashmere is on her knees. The day after Christmas she prayed for Cassidy out loud, at the TV. *Povera.* On the Innocents she asked me to sit for the rosary, and said the intentions — for Danny, for Pop, who went in, for the nun, and for Cassidy. I told her the name’s Skye. She said Cassidy. New Year’s: lentils, a spoon each, *per i soldi*. The Befana left me coal in one of Danny’s old socks. Sugar. At the door she found me a twenty and prayed for both of us. *Tutt’e due.* Thursday night I sent Gina the name: Mary Catherine. At breakfast Nonna said *Maria Caterina* nine times, and cried the good kind, and lit a candle for her at St. Brigid’s.

s10.slug: FRIDAY · 4:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE 4TH-FLOOR LOUNGE — THE GAG
body: Doug is waiting at the top of the stairs in socks and a Horde T-shirt, and he says “Duuuuude” before Jack is off the last step, with every vowel he owns. Room 420 has a gap in it where Doug’s desk chair used to be, until Tuesday, when Doug stood on the chair to kill a moth. The fourth-floor lounge has a spare futon frame. The raid is at seven.
“You didn’t bring me one,” Doug says on the way down the hall. “The taco. I said on the internet.”
“It was eleven at night on the Pacific Coast Highway, Doug.”
“Dude. They have *foil*.”
“Also, dude.” Doug lowers his voice to what he believes is a whisper. “Caleb says you and Lena went full Springer at Hale’s. Like, chairs.”
“Nobody threw anything, Doug.”
“He said the dog left the room.”
“The dog stayed.”
“Dude,” Doug says, with deep respect for the dog.

The lounge has one tall window, and the sun is low enough now to come straight in through it and lay a bar of gold across the carpet and up the wall where the futon frame leans, all slats and dowels. On the television bolted up in the corner, with the sound turned down to a murmur, the President is at a lectern in a hotel ballroom taking questions from rows of House Republicans, a replay from the morning; the banner under him says Baltimore. Yusuf is on the arm of the couch with a paperback. On the couch is Laney, with her laptop on her knees, and beside her Lena, in socks, with her feet up under her and a legal pad against her knees and a pen going. Greene’s *The End of the Affair* lies shut on the coffee table in front of her with a bookstore receipt sticking out of the back cover.

From the doorway he gets the end of something. Laney has turned on the cushion toward Lena, low and pleasant and steel all the way through: “— not what you *meant*, sugar. What you *said*. The words, in order, like a recipe —”
“I told you what I said.” Lena doesn’t look up from the pad. “He’s the one telling it different.”
Then Laney sees Doug, and past Doug the doorway, and says “*Futon!*” brightly, to nobody, and goes back to her screen.
He knows which *he*. He has nothing to add to it.
Jack didn’t check. It’s his floor; 217 has a floor of its own. He crosses to the far wall and gets his hands under his end of the frame.
“Yusuf won’t take the other end,” Doug says. “He says it’s a matter of conscience.”
“I said it’s a matter of my back.” Yusuf turns a page. He was at Hale’s on Wednesday, three chairs down, and he hasn’t looked up from the book since Jack came in. “Also I’m in mourning.”
“For the *Catcher in the Rye* guy,” Doug tells Jack.

“People have been coming up to me since breakfast like I’m the next of kin.” Yusuf tips the paperback up so the cover shows: *Nine Stories*, an old drugstore copy with the spine broken in three places. “I never read *Catcher*. I read the good one.”
“Dude, *Catcher*’s the good one. It’s the one with the hat.”
“It’s the one everybody read,” Yusuf says. “That’s a different thing.”

Priya goes past the doorway with a laminate under her arm, stops, comes back one step and says into the room, “Per the Residential Life Handbook, lounge furniture is *lounge* furniture, Doug.” Doug holds up a pink carbon with her signature at the bottom of it. Priya reads it to the end, including the fine print. She wrote it. “The fifth,” she says. “Not the sixth, Doug.” She takes the laminate on down the hall toward 401.
They have the frame off the wall and are turning it end for end, slowly, to clear the television, when Laney stops scrolling.
“Oh,” Laney says. “Oh, no. Oh, *bless* her heart, no.”

She clicks, and the screen fills with a picture. Jack knows it from across the room by its colors. She reads the caption aloud in the voice of a girl reading the winner’s card at Miss Texas, every word of it, slowing for the parenthesis: “*— we agree on each other* —”

Laney puts one hand to her throat. With the other she lifts the laptop off her knees and holds it out level at the end of her arm, like a tray she has been asked to carry out of a burning building, and then she dies. It is not quick. She goes over sideways across the far arm of the couch by stages, a dying swan in a Pi Lam sweatshirt: the back of her free wrist to her forehead, one leg rising, the toes pointed, the knee giving way, the laptop held up above her the entire time without a wobble, until she is hanging upside down off the arm with her hair on the carpet.

“I can’t,” she says. “I *can’t*. Tacos. She posted *tacos* at him. With a *parenthesis*.” Her head drops the rest of the way back. “Somebody call Tammy Price in Dallas and tell her her baby girl died of a taco. In California. Which she *warned* me about.”
And Lena laughs.

She has her mouth shut on it, hard, her lips pressed together, and it gets out anyway, through her nose: one short, loud, unlovely snort, the kind a person lets go of in the third pew at a funeral. Her eyes go wide at it. She is furious with her nose, and it’s all over her face, and behind the fury her mouth comes open anyway and the rest of it starts up out of her, real and helpless, her shoulders going —
— and her eyes come up over Laney’s hip and find the doorway, and find Jack in it with his end of the futon.

It goes out of her face from the top down. Her eyes first, then the color, then her cheeks; her mouth is the last part of her to get the news, still open on the shape of the laugh after the rest has gone, and then it closes too. She takes the cap off the coffee table and puts it on her pen and presses until it clicks. She picks up the Greene and sets it down again square to the edge of the table, and leaves her hand on the cover.

Upside down, Laney’s grip on the laptop has started to go, and Lena reaches up and takes it from her before it can hit the carpet, and looks at the screen to shut it, and doesn’t shut it. Under the picture the News Feed runs on down the screen, and from the doorway Jack can see the next story in it: the little square of his own new picture, and a line of gray text under it he doesn’t need to read. He read it at three o’clock this morning.

Lena’s eyes go down the screen and stop near the bottom. Her mouth closes on nothing. Then she shuts the laptop until it clicks, and sets it on the cushion beside her, and puts her hand flat on the lid.
It isn’t hers to read. It goes through him as irritation, small and sharp, and then there’s a futon to move.
“Lift on three,” Doug says. “Dude. *Three.*”

Laney is still hanging off the end of the couch, and she isn’t looking at the laptop anymore, or at Lena. She’s looking at Jack, down the length of the room: a long look, unreadable, her face going red from hanging upside down. Contempt, he figures; he’s had two weeks of it. He takes his end up on three.

They get it through the door on the second try. Doug walks backward with the light end, steering by his heels, and Jack has the heavy end and carries it down the corridor like it weighs what a broom weighs, past the trash chute and Priya’s bulletin board and the door of 412. At the turn Doug says, “Dude, *pivot*,” drawing it out to the length of a sentence, and Jack pivots, and the corner of the frame finds the doorjamb of 420 and takes out a chip of paint the size of a quarter.

Doug puts a fingertip on the bare wood. “That was there,” he says. “Dude. That was *there* before.” Inside, on his thirteen-inch, a tauren in plate armor stands by himself in the snow of Northrend, waiting for seven o’clock.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus. The Advent party: I kept the whole room between us all night. She brought coffee to the white elephant, and I got it. Stole my 8-Ball. Won an argument about ‘Joy to the World’ with Isaac Watts. Didn’t play. Julian did. Friday night, half past twelve, she knocked on 412; Theo said the library. At the Mañanitas she told me about Juan Diego, who took the long way around the hill. Thirteen and oh. She texted me the number. After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something. Better not tell you now. Geminids from the roof without me. At Hale’s oral she’d answered him in Augustine — said my sentence was his. She defended it and won, and told him to ask where I say yes at two in the morning. Julian kissed her goodbye at his car; he’s going to New Orleans for New Year’s. Friday she knocked with two coffees and a list of every place. She played the basement piano for me, properly. Taught me a secret in the O Antiphons. Pecan at Gloria’s counter; fourteen and oh is ordained. On the Lighthouse porch she said it plain: I’d never not answered her before. Never missed Sully’s. Always came to her, whatever it was — and now I stay away. She knows something’s hurting. She didn’t make me say what. Walked past the last house to the Point for the first time all semester. The bonfires on the levee on Christmas Eve — call her from the garage. On the roof I nearly said it. The 8-Ball said ask again later. She gave me the tin to keep. I gave her Benedict. At the checkpoint she turned around and said something I couldn’t hear. Christmas week: her sister had the baby in the third quarter of the Dallas game, while they were still undefeated, so Beau didn’t get a vote. Lucille Odile — both grandmothers. Lena’s the godmother. Then they lost. The 8-Ball said very doubtful. She texts me the O Antiphons at dusk. Monday night she called at ten to one to argue about Pius, and won the point fair. I told her I’ve been sleeping in Danny’s bed. She said somebody ought to. When the Pope went down she texted within the minute: is he alright, are you. Christmas Eve she held the phone up to a bonfire on the levee so I could hear it burn. After Midnight Mass she wrote from the steps of Holy Rosary: an hour behind me, like she said. She’d mailed me *The Moviegoer* before the last night. Christmas night she told me how Réveillon went, and about the place her mother sets for her grandmother. Then she said her mama worked at Memorial. Nothing else. Holy Family: they lost to Tampa in overtime — ‘They’re resting.’ Fr. Dom took the short form; hers read the long one, and we’re not discussing it. Sunday night we whispered for two hours because Nonna was asleep in her chair, and she whispered too, from her back steps. I read her her own margins; she argued with the girl who wrote them. I told her Dad went in. ‘And Danny drank it.’ Julian calls at ten his time. Tuesday she called from behind the register at her father’s market — home field; her father’s making the musician a gumbo. I told her what Danny asked about the third. If Pop won’t get out of the truck, she says, I get in. She said she wouldn’t call as much. Then she said she’d call. Wednesday nothing. Thursday at dawn, the morning after Julian landed, she called from the river with beignets. She said she’d call. She asked if I asked Ma who the candle was for. No. You don’t. New Year’s Eve she texted at my midnight, an hour early for her. At hers it came the second the year turned — before the fireworks. I know what that means. Then the river on fire, and Julian beside it. New Year’s Day I called her from the garage at the half, and she said, You called *me*. Saturday night she called the house — Ma answered and talked to her for ten minutes. Two hours on the kitchen phone, her mother’s cordless dying twice. Her grandmother made the christening gown for Luc in 1985; it rode out the storm in Mémère’s cedar chest in Breaux Bridge. She had me be the priest so she could practice the promises. She thinks Binx doesn’t stop looking — he stops looking by himself. I told her Danny asked me something I can’t answer yet; she didn’t ask what. She asked how California was. ‘Come back, Youngstown.’ Two hours, and she never said Julian’s name. Lucille was baptized in the third quarter, and she didn’t get one word wrong. After that I called every night. Twelfth Night she got the baby in the king cake. Friday she said she hasn’t been fair to Julian, and she’s going to fix it. Sunday she landed: come find me tomorrow. Monday I couldn’t find her — not at 217, not at the twelve-ten. She came into Hale’s seminar a step behind him with a king cake, and the only chair left was next to mine. She was polite to me for fifteen minutes. Then Dido. Tuesday morning Julian put up a picture from their dinner Monday — birthday dinner, two days late. She’s tagged. She’d said call me after. I didn’t. At the mailboxes she asked about my break, and I told her as far as Denver, and Ma’s words about the coffee. ‘Tell her I’m glad.’ The baptism was lovely. Tuesday night at St. Brendan’s she had the whole thing organized by half past eight, in a whisper, and put me on the table with Becca. When the TV said trapped she left the room. Julian went. Wednesday at the table she met Skye. She said no pictures at the table, and I argued with her about it in front of everybody. That night at the desk: Skye’s envelope was the biggest. ‘Tell her thank you. From Newman.’ Thursday she took the far end of Hale’s table before anybody got there. She moved the Saints to Sully’s. Saturday in the back hall she said she changed her mind, and stood up for Laney, and said Skye gave a good performance, and wouldn’t say what she meant. At Atlanta she kept my chair till the half. At ten after three she told me the time. Wednesday at three in the morning, the aftershock, in the Fishbowl: she said I could stop whatever I’m doing. I don’t know what I’m doing. Thursday Hale read her whole name off his list. She told him Lena. Saturday she ran the van to San Francisco. Six hours, row three. She asked me if I was happy. I said yes. At the end of the Walk I asked her how she had the nerve to be mad at me. She didn’t answer. She thanked me for coming and left. Monday, when Caleb said I was on a blog, she turned a page. Hale gave her Sarah Miles to prosecute and me Sarah to defend. Wednesday at his house, with the President on, she didn’t drink her wine. A website on Monday, a bed on Tuesday, an iPad before lunch — she had the whole week. She said she had to find out about my girlfriend from a Facebook status, when we talked every single day for weeks. I told her that’s what I meant in San Francisco: she as good as told me to. She says she said no such thing — that I’m lying to win an argument about a book. I was on the other end of that phone. I said it was the night for calling people liars, and got the date wrong, and she had the date. Then we said things we’ve never said. I told her she can’t forgive a status. She asked me if I still go up. Hale stood up and stopped it; the dog felt it through the floor. On her way out she told Hale Sarah let him believe he’d been replaced. She walked home up Del Playa with Laney. Friday in the lounge Laney found the taco picture. Lena laughed. Then she saw me. Then she read the rest of the screen and shut the laptop.

journal.title: Laney Price
journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass. Big/Little: Sloane is her big. On the front steps at one in the morning, in a PI LAM LITTLE shirt, with a balloon on her wrist, she told me about Kaylee Whitmore. Fifteen; Kaylee drove; they’d both been drinking and Laney let her. Preston Road. A culvert. A cast for six weeks that everybody signed. A month later, a doctor’s note for flying; she’d never been on a plane. Lena’s the only other one who knows. In the water at Pfeiffer Beach she caught my swan. It’s Theo’s. Her fourth Mass, up a mountain with the monks. Asked Lena how you light a candle, and lit one. Don’t you dare, she said. Halloween: Pope Joan, in a cardboard mitre with gold rickrack. Blessed Del Playa from the widow’s walk until Rafi’s father asked her to come down. Over a bullhorn. Best Couple, with Margot. Went missing with three pledges for most of the extra hour; Kevin found her at Lupe’s with a burrito. She’s not stupid. She’s hungry. Friday at the Situation Room: ‘Who’s that?’ ‘No one.’ Alarm Five: ‘Fireman. You’re dressed.’ Saturday on the laundry table with Theo and a legal pad, discussing finals. Somebody put an orange in her Ugg. She’s crying. The Advent party: black velvet, in mourning for Advent. A Texas thing in the punch; Kevin took her flask. Asleep on the porch swing by a quarter to eleven. The ninth at nine at the Anchor, with an agenda on an index card: pie, no questions. Sunday night she came out of my room with her laptop and went past me without a word. Since Sunday she hasn’t said a word to me. At the Haiti table she met Skye, and gave a hundred dollars to the clipboard. Wednesday night in the lounge she was keeping it short with Theo, for a nod. Then, to me, without turning her head: ‘Night.’ At Sully’s Skye brought her a present. She wore her own bells. She gave Skye advice, and I told her I’ve seen her work. Then she took a shot at Skye, and Skye was handling it, and I didn’t let her. I’ve never yelled at Laney before. The whole bar heard. Tuesday, after the storm, she came back down to the laundry room by herself, with a list: the airport, the status, Sully’s, the jacket, me. She asked what I’m doing. I told her the truth, which I haven’t told anybody. Then I left her standing there. I’m done with that room. Both of them. Friday on the west stairs she and Theo were doing a bit at each other about memory. I said morning. In the lounge she died across the arm of the couch over a picture of tacos. Then she looked at me a long time.

s10a.slug: FRIDAY · 4:58 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL
body: The landing windows in the east stairwell open six inches and then meet a bolt, put in by Residential Life the year somebody tried for seven. Jack pushes the one between four and three up until it meets it. Down in the lot the sun has gone long and gold across the windshields, and out on the asphalt a kid on a skateboard keeps trying the same curb: the wheels clack off it, a pause, again.

It comes up in his mouth first, and then in his fingers. The pack is in the inside pocket of the Carhartt with the lighter, and his hand is in there with it, holding it through the lining. The tin rides in the other pocket, against his hip, with its corners. Out in the lot the skateboard comes off the curb and goes down hard, and the kid lies on his back on the warm asphalt and hollers at the sky.

choices.text: *Light one.*
choices.key: On the east stairs Friday afternoon, you lit one.
response: He lights it in the gap with his shoulder against the frame and blows the first pull out through it, and the wind coming across the lot takes the smoke sideways, over the bike racks and the dumpsters and away toward the beach. He smokes it down with his forearms on the sill and the cold coming in over his wrists. He doesn’t think about anything.
He puts it out on the outside ledge and pockets the end. Below him the kid is up again, and lands the curb, and rolls off down the row of cars with both arms in the air.

choices.text: *Put it back.*
response: He takes his hand out of the jacket with nothing in it. The pack goes back down into the lining. He leaves the window up and stands in the cold coming through the gap with both hands on the sill, until his fingers quit asking, and the kid in the lot gets up and tries the curb again, and falls again, and gets up.

choices.text: *Open the tin. Count them.*
response: He takes out the tin instead and opens it on the sill. RELIQUARY, on the lid, in marker. He counts them in the last of the sun with one fingertip.
Eleven.
He shuts it and puts it back against his hip.

s11.slug: FRIDAY · 8:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL
body: The Fishbowl is the one room in Delgado with a glass wall, so that Residential Life can see in, and at half past eight on a Friday there is a great deal to see. On the television a woman with a gift for the afterlife is standing in a child’s bedroom telling a radiator *I know you’re still here*, and the room has its back to her. Priya’s table by the door has a new laminate up beside the guest ledger, ALL GUESTS SIGN IN. ALL., and in the ledger, in a round actress’s hand, under *Visiting* it says *412* and under *Purpose*, *ghost*. Priya studied it and let it stand.

Skye is on the arm of the middle couch in Jack’s flannel with the sleeves rolled to the elbow, telling Thursday to the room in parts. She does the host, whose every consonant is billed by the hour, and the host’s wife, who asked Jack the hardest question of the night and then thanked him for the answer with more wine. She does Glenn holding up his three lines like cue cards, and a showrunner on a staircase explaining a violinist, and Jack in Theo’s pinned trousers at the foot of the stairs being polite at forty donors for two hours. She does a shrimp on a spoon: its dignity, its rising dread. Doug lies on the carpet with a cushion under his head and says “On a *spoon*?” at the pauses. Kevin is on the floor against the radiator with his orgo open on his knees, not reading it. Theo, at the far end of the couch in the blue blazer, laughs on every beat and half a beat late. Jack was there. He wouldn’t have it any other way, since she tells it better than it went. She has had four hours of sleep and a morning of Corinne and she is the best thing in the room. Jack is aware this is not an objective assessment.
“I have a methodological concern,” says Margot, from the armchair, when the shrimp has been eaten.
“Put it next to the shrimp,” Skye says. “He’s been very good.”

“I’m in favor of argument. In the abstract I’m in favor of any room being argued with.” Margot has her notebook on the arm of the chair. “My difficulty is structural. Those people came to raise money for a right some of them have needed. You stood on the host’s staircase and handed the room they built for it to its opposition — charmingly, which is worse — and called it hospitality. I’d call it a platform. Then you put up a picture that says *we agree on each other*, which is a very pretty sentence and a political evasion. You don’t agree on each other. You agree on the shrimp.” She turns a page. “The only unambiguous statement anybody made all night was made at three in the morning, by Costigan, with his profile picture.”

“I didn’t hand them the room. I introduced them to him.” Skye tips her head at Jack. “They’d been arguing with a cartoon for thirty years. I thought they should meet the guy. Everybody in that house knew exactly where he stands, because I told them on the stairs, and I’m still voting for Barbara, and they had a better time than they’ve had since Dukakis. Glenn said so. Loudly.”

“Which is precisely what a hostess says. And staying is a statement too, whatever you meant by it. You can be perfectly sincere about staying in a room that thinks you’re wrong about the most important thing in your life. It still gets read as consent to the room.” Theo’s eyes go to Jack and back to the ghost.

At *a room that thinks you’re wrong* Kevin gets to his feet, says, “I need a pretzel,” and goes out through the glass door to the vending machine in the hall, where he stays, visible from every couch, selecting. He puts in a dollar, takes it back out, and puts it in again.
“The picture I put up instead was so I wouldn’t make *him* say something he doesn’t believe,” Skye says. “I don’t put words in people’s mouths. I get paid when other people do it to me.”
Margot looks at her for some time. “That is an ethics-of-attribution point,” she says, “and it’s a good one. I’ll give you the post. One point. I’m keeping the other one. It’s load-bearing.”
“Keep it,” Skye says. “I’ll come back for it.”
“I expect you will.” Margot slides the Fishbowl’s one clean mug across the coffee table to her. It has tea in it. Skye drinks it.
“Gil Abernathy, I’m told, wants a rematch,” Theo offers.
“Costigan.” Margot turns on him. “You have been very quiet for a man who was the evening’s entertainment.”
“I’m enjoying it,” Jack says. “And she’s right that it was a platform. I’d take it again.”
“Traitor,” Skye says.
“I’m on your side. She’s still right about the platform.”
“Keep going. I’m collecting.”

Margot ignores them both. “I would like it noted that the feminist outcome of the evening was a woman running a room full of donors from a staircase for two hours, on behalf of a man’s argument against the cause, and that I can’t use it.”
“Write it up anyway.”
“The Hostess Problem. With a footnote about the shrimp.”
Doug raises one hand from the carpet. “Was there, like, a little quiche?”
“A spoon, Doug.”
“Right. Right. On a spoon.”

“Since we’re on public statements.” Margot turns back a page in the notebook. “There are currently four versions of Wednesday at Hale’s circulating in this building. In the Serra Hall version, the dog required stitches.”
“Margot,” Theo says.
“I’m describing the literature.”
“The dog’s fine,” Jack says, and leaves it there. Skye, on the couch arm beside him, puts her hand on the back of his neck, and her thumb goes once along his hairline, and she asks him nothing.

The argument runs through a commercial break and out the other side into a second ghost. Skye, with her hand still on his neck and one bare foot found against his calf, leans in during the ads and says something into his ear in the host’s voice that he will be getting over until Tuesday. Then she watches the television for a while with her head on one side. “She has a *window* in that scene,” she says, “and she’s playing it to the radiator.”
“Dude, it’s a ghost,” Doug says.
“It’s still a window.”

At eleven by the clock over the sign-in table she slides off the couch arm and into her coat, and Priya already has the pen held out on its string. She signs herself out. Under *Purpose*, in the round hand: *achieved*. “Please come again,” Priya says, and then, frowning at herself, “That’s not on the laminate.” At the door she turns back to the room. “Saturday. Daylight. Bring the clipboard for Fenner,” she tells Jack, and kisses him, once, quick, in front of everybody, and Doug applauds alone.
“Thank you, Douglas.” She looks down the couch. “Ted.”
“Skye.”
“Sunday.”
“You told me. Twice,” Theo says, short, and it gets out the door before she does.

Through the glass Jack watches her cross the lobby, and Marcus at the front desk watch her all the way to the street door. In the hall Kevin has finally selected and is eating a pretzel, one at a time. When Jack turns around Theo has moved down the couch to him without seeming to move, and is watching the ghost.
“You stayed,” Theo says, low.
“She kept me there.”
“That’s worse, Costigan.” Now he looks over. “That’s *love*.”

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend. She has a faith column now, in the *Tide*, on a trial basis. If it’s boring they’ll kill it. She told me not to be boring. Came to Big Sur as an observer, for the monks — a functioning patriarchy in its natural habitat. Ran the *Tide*’s Ferrer follow-up from a minivan and wrote nothing down. Sunday at the coffee urn: ‘I’m not writing anything down.’ Halloween: Joan of Arc in duct tape, with her own haircut. Best Couple, with Pope Joan. She called it a category error and laughed anyway. Told me I’m surface acting. Hochschild, 1983. The flight attendants. On the stairs, about Julian: ‘He’s the healthiest thing in her life, Costigan.’ She meant it. Alarm Five: twenty-seven days; she’d said twenty-six. Out past one, four nights of six — she doesn’t sleep, she counts. Not writing it down. Sunday: UNEXPLAINED CITRUS. Nineteen on the solstice, four days early, under protest. Likes us. On the record. Lit a candle for research. Took Skye’s side about the rose. Goffman, 1956. Wrote TED in her notebook and underlined it. Gave to Partners In Health and sent the rest of us there — Farmer’s Catholic, sort of. Commented ‘Front stage.’ on my status. Wednesday night in the lounge, while Laney kept it short with Theo: keeping score. A page in her notebook says SKYE. Thursday at the Anchor she interviewed Skye for her column. She hated that it was good. Her column ran Thursday: ‘Front Stage.’ It’s good. I told her twice. Thursday she brought Salinger’s death to the window table like a lab result. Friday in the Fishbowl she took Skye on about the fundraiser: a room raised for a cause, handed to its opposition. Skye said she didn’t hand them the room, she introduced them to me, and she’s still voting for Boxer. Margot gave her one point and kept one. Four versions of Wednesday are going around Delgado, she says. Commented *Back region. Finally.* on the taco picture.

choices.text: “Yeah. It is.”
choices.key: In the Fishbowl Theo said staying for her was love. You said yes, it is.
response: Theo looks at him for a while, and then at the television, where a ghost is being helped toward the light. “Well,” he says. “Mazel tov.”

choices.text: “Put it on a plaque. Brass. Serif.”
choices.key: In the Fishbowl Theo said staying for her was love. You told him to put it on a plaque.
response: “I’ll have it engraved,” Theo says. “HE STAYED, EST. 2010. Margot will say brass is a choice.”
“Brass is a choice,” Margot says, from across the room, without looking up.
