choices.key: In the Fishbowl Theo said staying for her was love. You told him again she’s the answer.
response: Theo doesn’t argue. He finds the remote in the cushions and turns the ghost up.

body: A clear Saturday, and the town has come out to stand in it. The sky over the Point is scrubbed hard and pale, the storms have left the kelp in black heaps along the tide line, and out past the rocks the swell comes in from the northwest in long clean lines, with the wind off the land combing the spray back off their tops. Down by the dark Light the low wall is already warm through Jack’s jeans.

Pair 41 has set up at the north end of it: Fenner’s form on the clipboard, one pencil, a stopwatch signed out of the department with PROPERTY OF MORRO 1100 scratched into its back with a key, and a paper bag from the bakery on Seacliff Road that held four Danish at ten o’clock and holds one now. The method is Fenner’s. Pick a rock. Time each crest as it crosses the rock, ten in a row, write them down, do it again from the next station along the wall. Skye has the pencil because she has the handwriting. She also has his flannel from the Walk on, over a gray sweatshirt that says SWEETWATER ACADEMY CREW. She took it from wardrobe in 2008 and calls it the only honest thing she owns.
Out in the lineup a dozen surfers sit their boards in the swell, black in their wetsuits, waiting. One of them goes for a wave too early, and it goes on without him.

“He’s going to go for this one, Jim,” Skye says, very low, in the hush of a golf announcer at the eighteenth green, a man in a blazer who has never once raised his voice at a wave. “A bold choice. A young man’s choice.” Below them the young man comes up out of the white and shakes his hair out of his eyes. “He’ll want that one back.”
Jack clicks the stopwatch. “Eleven.”

“The young man is eleven.” She writes it down. “And now, Jim, the veteran. Gray at the temples. Look at that patience. He has waited forty minutes for this, and he’ll go home and tell his wife about it, and she won’t listen.” The older man drops into a clean right and rides it nearly to the rocks, and Skye breathes, “Oh, that’s *lovely*,” and writes down *twelve*.

They do ten. They move down the wall to the second station, past the white cross at the end of it, where last Sunday’s roses are still tied to the fence wire, gone brown on their kitchen string. They do ten more.

body.text: “This is the daylight column,” she says, writing down a set. “I’m living in it. It’s very bright. I don’t know how you people stand it.”
body.else: “This is daylight,” she says, writing down a set. “I’m told it’s good for you.”

body: “Margot’s four versions,” she says, writing down the next set. “Doug told me a fifth in the ad break. One of them has a dog in it.” She doesn’t look up from the form. “I’m not asking for yours. I just didn’t want you wondering whether I’d heard.”
“There was a dog,” Jack says. “It was fine.”
“There’s always a dog.” She clicks the pencil against the clipboard, once, and goes back to the swell.

Fenner wants to know why the Point breaks where it does, and Jack has the answer off the lecture slides: the shoal under the Point, the end of each wave that feels the bottom first and slows down, and the rest of the line swinging around to catch up with it, so that every set coming in off the open water bends toward the Point and stands up here, in front of them.
“So it bends toward the slow part,” Skye says.
“That’s refraction.”
“That’s the most romantic thing Fenner has ever said, and he said it about sediment.” She puts the pencil behind her ear and takes the last piece of Danish without offering it.
He tells her about the candle while she’s eating it: Nonna lit one. A tall one, up the side aisle at St. Brigid’s before the school Mass, with the whole family late for it.
“A candle,” Skye says. “For me.”
“For Maria Caterina.”

He says it the way Nonna says it, every vowel open, the *r* turned over once on the tongue. Skye stops chewing. She looks out at the lineup, where nothing is happening, for long enough that the veteran paddles back out past the break.

“Maria Caterina,” she says, finally, reaching for a bit, “sounds like a woman who runs a bakery and has opinions about your —” and that’s as far as she gets with it. She shuts her mouth on the rest and shakes her head at herself, and wipes one eye with the cuff of his flannel, fast, like it was spray.
“Say it again,” she says. “The Italian way.”
He says it again. She says it after him under her breath, and gets the *r* wrong, and then right.
When the next set is written down she taps the pencil on the clipboard. “I’m sitting where I sat last week,” she says, to the form. “Tomorrow.”
“Same pew.”
“Same pew.” She nods, a scheduling matter, settled, and that’s all either of them says about tomorrow.

Out at the first rock the swell lifts again, three lines deep, and he clicks the stopwatch. The first one feels the shoal and slows, and the rest of it comes around to meet it, and it breaks where it does. “Nine,” he says, and she writes it down.

journal.title: Oceanography 1
journal.text: Oceanography 1, Tuesdays and Thursdays at eleven, Morro Hall 1100. Rocks for Jocks, Wet. Skye took it too and didn’t tell me which science till she was sitting in the back row under the exit sign with the book. Fenner: seventy-one percent, and we have better maps of Mars. The ground is not where you left it, week two. Partners by seat, Thursday. Skye, till May. No trades. Our project is the Point — why it breaks where it does. Fenner: approved, don’t drown. Tuesday: half of Pair 41. Wednesday: field data from the lot in a storm — it wasn’t breaking where it does. It was breaking everywhere. Sunday: the Point open again — breaking where it does. Saturday at the Point with Fenner’s form and a stopwatch, timing the sets. Skye called the surfers like the last hole of a golf tournament. Breaking where it does.

s13.slug: SATURDAY · 6:15 PM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — THE OTHER TIE
body: The sun is down, and 412 is blue except for the desk lamp, and under the window the curb has begun to fill with heels.

Theo has tied the navy silk four times in the full-length mirror and undone it four times, and on the fifth he gets as far as the second turn, stops, and takes it off over his head. The hands that can deal a deck, split a lime with a thumbnail and open a Rioja with a shoe will not do this one thing tonight. He holds the tie out without turning around. “Costigan.”

Jack gets up off his bed. He is in jeans and a Marisol sweatshirt, off a short shift at the Anchor at five with the flat-top still in his hair, and he has nowhere to be, a fact he keeps finding in his pockets like a twenty.
“Last offer,” Theo says. “Pi Lam has a surplus of girls with minors in Italian.”
“I’m good.”

Jack stands behind him, the two of them in the mirror, Thursday with the parts swapped, and does it: over, under, through, the half-Windsor, drawn up to a finger’s width of the collar. “It’s a commitment,” he says, working the knot.

“Don’t quote me to me.” Theo lifts his chin for the collar. “The theme tonight is *A Night in the Alps*, in a county where it is sixty-eight degrees. The Alps are two thousand dollars of foam. There is a machine that makes snow. It is soap, Costigan, and at ten o’clock a girl in a strapless dress will run out into it with her arms up and be, for forty seconds, entirely happy, and I would not take that from her for anything.” Downstairs his date is waiting at the front desk.
He watches Jack’s hands in the glass. “Indulge me, Costigan. The call. January, your father’s garage. What did she actually say? Not the gist. The words.”
Jack’s hands stay on the knot. “We did this Thursday.”
“Thursday you picked a tie. We didn’t do this.”

So he gives it to Theo once, in order, flat as a box score. “She asked if I’d be around after. I said I had a thing. She said *then call me after. Eat something first.* And that she hadn’t been fair to him, and she was going to fix it.” He tugs the knot straight. “She fixed it. There was a picture Tuesday morning. Birthday dinner.”
“In that order?”
“In that order. I said it to a whole table on Wednesday, Theo. It’s done.”

Theo doesn’t answer that. On the dresser beside his cufflinks his iPhone lights up face-up with a text Jack can’t read from here, and Theo reads it upside down without picking it up, and types something short with one thumb, and turns the phone over. “Eight days,” he says, to the back of it.
“Till what?”
“The Super Bowl, Costigan. Some of us have plans to make.” He lifts his chin for the collar again. “Do you know what you’re going to say tomorrow? If she asks.”
Jack’s hands finish the knot. “She’s going to ask.”
“That’s not what I asked.”
In the mirror, over Theo’s shoulder, Jack has nothing to put in his face. He sets the collar down over the knot and smooths it with both thumbs, and Theo lets him, and they both study the tie.

Then the voice comes back on like a porch light. “I shall be at the Pi Lam house being asked what my father does, by people who know,” Theo says. “Don’t wait up. Or do, Father Jack. It’s a free country, and you have a lamp.” He takes the blazer off the chair, and goes.

Jack goes to the window. The moon is coming up over the ridge behind Engineering, full and still orange from the ground, so big it looks nearer than the ridge, and he watches it climb the oaks. At the bottom of the glass, at the edge of what he is looking at, Brooks Callahan’s black Tahoe is idling at the curb with its hazards going, and Laney comes down the Delgado steps under the porch light in gold sequins and a wrap she has no intention of wearing. Lena, in a gray sweatshirt, comes after her with the wrap over one arm. At the curb she takes the last inch of the zipper in both hands and finishes it, and Laney lifts her hair off her neck in the pageant gesture to let her. Then the Tahoe door, and Brooks around it, and the gold goes in, and an arm comes out of the back window for the wrap, and Lena puts it there. When the car pulls away the sweatshirt goes back up the steps.
The moon is clear of the ridge. Ma’s red tie has waited since Thursday. Jack hangs it over the back of the desk chair, where he will see it at seven.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Landed in the middle of the night — they wanded the baccalà in Pittsburgh. At the side door Christmas afternoon he said, Be careful, Costigan. Of what. All of it. New Year’s Eve, at nine his time, the party was already a disappointment. Wore Ma’s scarf in sixty-one degrees. A woman asked if he was in a band. Back from LA in the orange hat and Ma’s scarf. Says the hat is a family heirloom. Sunday night: ‘Congratulations, Costigan.’ ‘Go to sleep. Monday is going to be a long day.’ Tuesday morning he did the responses too: Lord, hear our prayer. Rushing Sigma Rho; ate a raw onion in front of the lacrosse team. Wednesday night he got a bid. A pledge now. Carries a raw egg named Hollis in a teacup; if it breaks, he’s out. At Sully’s: ‘She’s the best actress I know, Costigan. Never ask her if she’s acting.’ MLK Day he shoveled sand one-handed for Sigma Rho with Hollis in the other. At midnight Wednesday he pitched me a movie about a man whose friend got dumped and was with somebody else in a week. He said it twice. Hollis made his week. Theo’s in. He’s keeping the egg. Saturday he became a brother. Sunday he runs. He was correct to Lena for seven hours at Sully’s and sent me the end of it. He started on Julian, and I told him to stop. Monday he asked me, hypothetically, where a man who doesn’t go to Sully’s watches the Super Bowl. Made himself my plus-one to Hale’s, with a bottle that had a story. Tuesday morning I told him I think she’s the answer. He wanted a pamphlet, framed. Then he said nobody ever asked her to be that, and an answer is heavy for the person you hand it to. At Hale’s door Laney told him that wasn’t about a book. He said no. At midnight, to the ceiling: don’t ever make me watch that again. Thursday he dressed me for the Palisades: his charcoal suit, pinned, and a half-Windsor — a commitment, like a coat. In the mirror he said I was good at it Wednesday, and that’s what he didn’t like. Friday: “You stayed.” She kept me there. “That’s love.” Saturday I tied his for the Pi Lam formal. He wanted the January call word for word. I gave it to him once. He asked if I know what I’m going to say tomorrow, if she asks.

s14.slug: SATURDAY · 10:50 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE — THE BLUFF STAIRS, FULL MOON
body: Through the screen door of Sol’s house Tomás has something old going on the stereo, brushes on a snare and a steel guitar and a man singing high and thin, and it comes out across the porch and goes on past them down the bluff toward the water. The moon is up over the ocean, full, white as a plate, bright enough that Jack can read the Surfrider sticker on the porch rail. Sol’s swing is back on its hooks on the new chain, and Skye is in it with her knees pulled up inside a cream fisherman’s sweater that comes to the middle of her thighs, bare legs, bare feet, pushing herself off the boards with one toe.
“You’re late,” she says.
“It’s ten-fifty. You said ten-thirty.”
“I said ten-thirty and I meant ten. I wanted you early.”

He doesn’t have an excuse, so he gives her news instead: he tied Theo’s tie tonight. She stops the swing with her heel to hear it, and he gives her all of it: the foam Alps, the soap snow, the girl who will run out into it at ten o’clock with her arms up.

“Ted at a formal,” she says. “He’ll be the only man there with a pocket square and an exit plan. We went to a premiere together when we were twelve and he left during the speeches. Out a bathroom window. In a clip-on.”
“He gave me a speech about the snow.”
“That’s crying, for Ted.” She gets up off the swing. “Come see the stairs. Tomás fixed the bottom one. He wants it noticed.”

The bluff stairs go down the cliff behind the house in three crooked flights, gray boards gone soft with salt and a two-by-four for a rail, and at the bottom the beach lies pale under the moon all the way to the Point, and the surf comes in loud and white and slides back hissing. She goes first, barefoot, not holding the rail. Four steps down she stops and turns around on the step below him, so that her eyes come level with his, and kisses him.

It goes on a long time. The music comes down the bluff in pieces, whenever the wind allows it. He gets his hands up under the sweater and there is nothing under it but her: the small of her back warm under the wool and cold at the edges where the night has got in. He spreads his hands over her shoulder blades and brings her up the step into him, and she makes a sound against his mouth. Her own hands go inside his flannel and up under his T-shirt, and they are freezing, and he flinches, and she hums, pleased with herself, and keeps them there, spread over his ribs, until they warm.

His thumbs find the bottom edge of her ribs and follow it around, slowly, and her breath goes short against his cheek. She puts her mouth to his throat under the hinge of his jaw, teeth and then not teeth. The step is too narrow for two people. Her thigh is between his, and the rail is in his back, and when she leans her weight into him the flight of stairs creaks from top to bottom. He hears himself say her name into her hair.

They don’t make it down the rest of the way so much as arrive. At the bottom she pulls him onto the sand, and it is cold through his jeans and cold under his palms, and she comes down into his lap facing him with her knees in the sand on either side and the sweater riding up her thighs, and kisses him again, slower, both hands on his face. The moon is behind her on the water. He has his hands under the wool on the warm bare skin of her back, and every part of him knows where they would go next, and wants them there. There is her weight, and the cold, and the sound she makes when his thumbs go along her ribs again. She shifts in his lap, once, and they both feel where that would go, and she stops, and puts her forehead down on his and laughs, unsteadily, at both of them.
He pulls back far enough to see her. Her mouth is wet and her hair is full of wind and moon, and the next words are coming up in him before he has them, and he knows exactly what they are.
“Skye —”
She puts two fingers over his mouth.
“*Tomorrow*,” she says. Her breath isn’t steady. Her fingers are. “I gave my word. You don’t get to make me break it the night before.”

choices.text: *Say it anyway, against her fingers: “Tomorrow, then.”*
choices.key: Saturday night on the bluff you almost asked. Skye kept her word — tomorrow — and you said it back against her fingers.
response: “Tomorrow, then,” he says, against her fingers, so that she feels it more than hears it.

She takes the fingers away and kisses the place where they were. Then she gets up off him, and pulls him up by both hands, sand pouring out of his flannel, and at the foot of the stairs she holds his face in both hands while Tomás’s record comes down to them on the wind.

choices.text: *Kiss her fingers. Let her keep her word.*
choices.key: Saturday night on the bluff you almost asked. Skye kept her word, and you let her.
response: He kisses her fingers where they lie over his mouth, and that is his answer.
She takes them back and looks at them in the moonlight. “That isn’t fair either,” she says. She climbs off him and sits down on the bottom step in the sweater, and points up the stairs with her chin.
He goes up on his own. At the top, with the screen door letting the record out again, he looks down, and she’s sitting on the bottom step with her arms around her knees.

choices.text: *Ask anyway.*
choices.key: Saturday night on the bluff you asked anyway. Skye said no — kissing you through it — for your sake.
response: He takes her hand away from his mouth by the wrist and keeps it, and asks. He doesn’t dress it up. “I don’t want to wait till tomorrow.”

“No,” she says, into his mouth, laughing, kissing him through it, “no, no, absolutely not, no —” and keeps on until he cracks too, his forehead against hers. “You’d be sorry by the Gospel,” she says, “and I’d have to sit there and watch you be sorry.”
She gets up, and hauls him up after her, and pushes him up the first three steps by the seat of his jeans.

s15.slug: SUNDAY · 11:30 AM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR — THE FOURTH SUNDAY
body: The 11:30 is the Mass for the late, the hungover and the young families, and the sun comes in through the high clear windows of St. Brendan’s in long slanting bars and lies across all three. Out in the courtyard somebody has taped a Catholic Schools Week banner to the parish-hall door in blue and gold, and it has already begun to curl. Jack is wearing Ma’s red tie. It has finally got its pew.

Skye is already in the one where she sat last week, halfway up on the Mary side, on the aisle so he can get out. She has on a gray cardigan buttoned to the throat over a white collar, and her hair pinned up, and no makeup he can find. When she leans forward to put the kneeler down a price tag rides up out of the back of it on its plastic thread — $68, and the name of a store on State Street — and he reaches over and tucks it back under the wool with one finger.
She keeps her eyes front. “I bought it for this,” she says. “Don’t look at it.”

Mrs. Fitch’s bulletin is in the hymnal rack, clip-art angels blowing trumpets around the Mass times, and while the procession comes up the aisle Skye takes it out and reads it to the end — the Knights’ pancake breakfast, the CYO car wash, the prayer list — and puts her finger on a name under PLEASE PRAY FOR, a stranger in Lompoc, and keeps it there through the opening hymn.
Jeremiah first, read by a man from the choir: *before I formed you in the womb I knew you*. Skye’s eyes come sideways to Jack, a week after San Francisco, and go back.
Bridget McNulty from Newman reads the second reading, in a navy skirt, holding the edges of the big book like a railing.
*“Love is patient, love is kind.”*

She goes on down the list of everything it isn’t — not jealous, not pompous, not rude — and Jack stops at the first word. *Patient.* He looks at Skye’s hands. They’re folded in her lap, right thumb over left, the fingers that were over his mouth twelve hours ago lying still on her knee. All week she has kept the word she gave him on Monday, and she has kept it better than he would have.

Father Osei reads the Gospel himself: Nazareth turning on its own boy. *Amen, I say to you, no prophet is accepted in his own native place.* They drive him out of town to the brow of the hill to throw him off it, *but he passed through the midst of them and went away.* Osei closes the book and stands at the ambo with no notes.

“They could not hear him in Nazareth because they already knew him,” he says. “The carpenter. Joseph’s boy. The one who borrowed a ladder and did not bring it back. It is very hard to be heard by people who are sure they know you — and notice that he does not argue with the hill. He passes through the midst of them, and he goes on.”
He sits down.
Skye leans over. “That’s it?” she whispers. “He’s done?”
“He doesn’t go long.”
“I’ve had longer notes from a grip.”

At the sign of peace the old man in the pew behind them shakes Skye’s hand like a deacon and says, “Peace be with you, young lady,” and she says, “And also with you,” without hesitating, the response she learned last Sunday, and turns to Jack and takes his hand in both of hers and just holds it.

At Communion Gus Ferreira brings the organ down to almost nothing, and the choir starts the Taizé chant that goes round and round, *Ubi caritas et amor*, and the ushers come up the side aisle a pew at a time. When it’s their pew Skye stands and steps out into the aisle to let him by, and he goes.
This week nobody passes the plate over him.

The line moves at its usual crawl, a man in front of him with a toddler asleep on his shoulder, a girl in a Marisol rowing jacket behind. On the way up he goes back over last night once, honestly, as they taught him for his First Communion, and comes out where she left him: at the bottom of the bluff stairs, with her fingers over his mouth and nothing gone anywhere. Osei is at the head of the center aisle with the ciborium. Jack opens his hands.
“The Body of Christ.”
“Amen.”

He has done this since he was seven, in Danny’s old shoes with Kleenex in the toes, and every time it is the same and it is never the same. He steps to the side and receives, and crosses himself, and turns back down the aisle with his hands folded, and the peace comes up in him that he has never been able to account for and has given up trying to.
When he gets back to the pew she’s kneeling.

Last Sunday she sat through all of it with her back straight and her hands in her lap, a guest at somebody else’s dinner. Today her hands are together on the back of the pew in front, and she doesn’t look at him as he slides in past her. She is looking at the altar like Nonna looks at her stove: hard, memorizing where everything is, so she could find it again in the dark.
He kneels beside her, close enough that their shoulders touch through the wool, and feels her breath catch once against his arm, and steady.
At the door after the recessional Osei is shaking hands in the sun with his stole still on, the late crowd going past him down the steps into the courtyard. He takes Skye’s hand first.
“Skye.”
“Father.”

He keeps her hand while he looks at Jack. The look is not gentle, and not soft, and it lasts about as long as a handshake. He doesn’t say anything. He lets go of her hand and turns to the family behind them.

Mrs. Fitch is at the foot of the steps in her good coat with a foil-covered sheet pan in both arms, on her way to the courtyard. She stops in front of Skye. “Lemon bars are *Sunday*,” she tells her, as if Skye had suggested otherwise, and goes on.
“I didn’t say anything,” Skye says.
“She knows.”
Skye takes his arm on the steps. The stone is warm under the sun, and the bells haven’t started yet, and she looks up at him in Ma’s tie. “Feed me,” she says.

journal.title: Fr. Gabriel Osei
journal.text: Newman chaplain. Kumasi, Ghana. Used to be a doctor. Limps and doesn’t mention it. Plays chess like he’s got all night and highlife like the neighbors owe him money. Told me a proverb about funerals. I laughed. That was apparently the point. Said Nonna’s Mass himself at the 12:10, like he promised. Gave me a card for her: ‘A grandmother likes paper.’ Blessed Hale’s deaf dog with his hand on its ribs, where it could hear. Finished Hale’s limerick for him. Laughed for a full minute at Becca’s crab. All Souls, at the book: ‘Write them all. He has a large book and a long memory.’ Saturday, behind the screen, one question: do I want to stop seeing her, or stop what happens. Change the hour. Keep her in the daylight. The Advent party: got the spray tan. Confiscated the mistletoe — he requested. At the sink he told me about the waiting room in Kumasi. His door is the one with the light on. Saturday, behind the screen: love wills the good of the other — and that’s why it’s dangerous. Gaudete: rejoice is a command. Wednesday, behind the screen: I’m not avoiding the occasion, I’m scheduling it. Distance is a mercy; use it. Blessed us both for the road on the Newman steps. Come back. The first day back I gave him Father Dom’s message: we’ll see. He laughed. I told him I went at home. The night of the earthquake he asked the bishop if he could spare an old doctor. The bishop couldn’t spare a young priest. His friend Yaw from medical school is in Port-au-Prince — alive, operating in a parking lot. Saturday at three-thirty the light was on. Sunday he read Cana. Yaw has a generator now. Sunday at the 11:30 I didn’t go up. At the door I introduced him to Skye. He said her name. Then he said Wednesday, eight o’clock. Wednesday at eight the light was on, and he waited. Not gentle this time. I told him I think she’s the answer, and he asked: to what question? I didn’t have it. He said on Monday it was she who kept my Sunday, not me. I told him I called a friend a liar at a table, and went for the places that hurt. Two sins, he said, and I confessed the one I’m sure of. He said he’d be less sure, if he were me. I told him I’d spoken for him on Monday. He let most of it stand: what’s good between us is good, and the near occasion was the room and the hour and the door. He said I took his daylight at noon with the door shut. Neither one cancels the other. And if I make her the answer, I’ll make her the occasion. The absolution isn’t a curtain between Fridays. He said Ma asked me the right question. He asked what will be different when I leave. Absolved me anyway. Penance: the Sower, slowly — the thorns. Then: go home tonight. The Fourth Sunday: a prophet’s never welcome in his own country. Skye watched me go up. At the door he said “Skye,” and she said “Father,” and he looked at me about as long as a handshake. He didn’t say anything.

choices.text: *Take her to the Anchor.*
choices.key: After Mass you took Skye to the Anchor for lunch, and Gloria rated her.

choices.text: *Stay for coffee hour.*
choices.key: After Mass you stayed for coffee hour with Skye, and Tyler asked her consent to a novena.

s15a.slug: SUNDAY · 12:45 PM · THE ANCHOR — THE COUNTER
body: By daylight the Anchor is somebody else’s diner. The harbor comes in white through the front windows and finds every scratch in the counter, the booths are full of fishermen’s families in church clothes and a softball team in a winning mood, and Gloria is behind the register on a Sunday noon, which happens about as often as Easter, because the day girl is having a baby in Ventura. Rudy is on the line for the same baby. His transistor is on the shelf over the pass, turned low to a man selling tires in Spanish, and the rosary inked around his left wrist goes in and out of the steam.
Gloria has two coffees down before they’re all the way onto their stools, and looks at Skye, at the pinned-up hair and the buttons done to the throat, with the pencil going behind her ear.
“My granddaughter made me watch your program,” she says. “The Thursday one. With the lake.”
“I’m so sorry,” Skye says.
“Don’t be sorry, hon. Be smarter. That girl of yours should’ve left that boy in the second season. He’s got no chin, and he lies to her in a canoe.”
Skye sets down her coffee. “I *said* that. At the table read. I said Cassidy would push him out of the canoe and row back by herself. They gave the line to the lake.”

Gloria nods slowly, as if this confirms something she has long suspected about the lake. “Nights in here you were boysenberry,” she says. “I remember.” She looks again, with the harbor light full on Skye’s face. “Daytime you’re a different pie. Peach. Peach in January.” She writes on her pad without asking what they want. “You don’t believe it’s real, and there it is on the plate.”
She goes. Skye turns on her stool. “Is that good? Tell me that’s good.”
“She told me lattice-top. Pretty on top, everything leaking underneath.”
“So she’s met you.”

The peach comes out of a can under a lattice, warm, with the ice cream already giving up on top of it, and Gloria stands at the end of the counter with her arms folded until Skye has had the first bite and said so. Over it Skye tells him Corinne called during the Gospel. The network has two seats at a thing tonight, a Grammy party, and Corinne had a dress in mind and a reason it would help.
“I said I had church,” Skye says.
“Church was this morning.”
“I didn’t say which.” She cuts the point off her slice with the side of her fork. “She said, *You’ve been.* I said, *I’m going again.*”
She puts the point on his plate.

On Glenwood Avenue the point is the best bite, and there has been no peace at that table over who gets it since Nonna was a bride. She has given it away without looking up, the way you’d pass somebody the salt, and gone on talking about Corinne’s dress, and he eats the point of a canned-peach pie as slowly as a man can eat anything.
At the pass Rudy sets down a second slice, on the house, and slides it along the steel to her, and goes back to his tires without a word. Skye turns around to look at him.
“He likes you,” Gloria says, going by with the pot. “Don’t make a thing of it.”

At two o’clock the lot behind the Anchor is hot and smells of fish scales and asphalt, and the Saab has been sitting in the sun with its top down. Skye gets in behind the wheel and shrugs out of the gray wool and drops it on the back seat, and then she is in the white blouse with the sleeves pushed up, putting on her sunglasses. She looks at him over the top of them.
“Tonight,” she says.
He’s standing in the lot with his hands in his pockets and Ma’s tie pulled loose at his collar.
“Tonight.”

s15b.slug: SUNDAY · 12:40 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE OLIVE-TREE COURTYARD — COFFEE HOUR
body: Coffee hour happens under the olive trees whenever it isn’t raining, and it isn’t, so the courtyard is full: two card tables, an urn of coffee that tastes of the urn, the late crowd standing around in its good shoes, children going in circles around the fountain with powdered sugar on their mouths. Mrs. Fitch has the end of the second table with the foil off and the lemon bars cut in exact squares. She puts one on a napkin and holds it out to Skye.
“Thank you,” Skye says.
“Mm,” says Mrs. Fitch, and watches her eat it.

Tyler Brandt finds them by the fountain with a manila folder under his arm. “Brother,” he says to Jack, and to Skye, “Miss Callender. Mrs. Fitch says a novena requires the consent of the subject. I took it up with Father. Father said Mrs. Fitch is right, as a rule.” He opens the folder. “So I drew something up.”

body.title: ST. BRENDAN’S NEWMAN CENTER — NOVENA: CONSENT OF THE SUBJECT
body.text:
I, the undersigned, consent to be prayed for by Tyler Brandt (and anybody he can get) for nine (9) consecutive days, beginning Monday, February 1, 2010, for the following intention: *the pair of you.* I understand that I may withdraw my consent at any time, and that it will not stop him.

Signature of subject: ______________
Witness: ______________

body: Skye reads it to the bottom with her lips pressed together. “What’s my billing?”
“Ma’am?”
“Is it the pair of us, or the pair of you? Am I above the line?”
Tyler looks at the form with real concern. “It’s — alphabetical? To God?”
“Callender,” Skye says to Jack. “I go first.”
“Do I sign too?” Jack says.
“You’re covered, Brother. You’re Catholic.”

Tyler holds out a pen. Skye props the folder on the edge of the fountain and signs on the line, fast, with a flourish: *Skye*, the big loop under it running out past the margin, the same autograph she has put on ten thousand eight-by-tens. Then she turns, and holds the pen out to Mrs. Fitch for the witness line.

Mrs. Fitch accepts the pen after a moment and writes *D. Fitch* under the loop in the hand that does the bulletin, small and upright, and hands the pen back to Tyler without a word, and Tyler holds the form against his chest like a diploma, and Jack has to turn around and look at the fountain until his face is his own again.

Peter Haddad comes past with the spare urn in both arms, sees them, and stops, and sets it down on the lip of the fountain to say it properly. “Brother. For the record, Newman isn’t taking sides about Wednesday.” He looks at Skye and colors and nods to her. “I’ve said that to everybody who’s asked me. A lot of people have asked me.”
“Thanks, Peter.”
Peter picks the urn back up and carries it off toward the parish hall. Skye watches him go, and finishes her lemon bar, and wipes her fingers on the napkin one at a time.

Across the courtyard Becca Lindell is holding somebody’s baby by the bench around the big olive. She sees Jack, and lifts the baby’s fist and waves it at him, and then her own hand, and goes back to the baby.
Under the far tree Father Osei is out of his vestments with a paper cup, listening to an old man in a Korea veterans cap. He sees them. He doesn’t come over.
“Corinne called during the Gospel,” Skye says, with the second lemon bar. “The network has two seats at a Grammy party tonight. She had a dress in mind and a reason it would help.”
“What’d you tell her?”
“I said I had church.” She licks sugar off her thumb. “She said, *Church is in the morning.* I said I have a lot of church.”

At two o’clock the bells go for nothing in particular and the courtyard empties out toward the lot. The Saab has been sitting in the sun at the far end of it with its top down. Skye gets in behind the wheel and pushes her sunglasses up into her pinned hair, and Jack stands at the open passenger door with one hand on the top of it. He’s walking up the hill; she’s going home to learn lines.
“Tonight,” he says.
She looks at him from behind the wheel, buttoned to the throat for Mass.
“Tonight.”

s16.slug: SUNDAY · 4:10 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL — GLENWOOD
body: A wrist corsage lies on the third step down, white, browned at the edges of the petals, left over from somebody’s Saturday. The four o’clock sun comes through the wired glass at the turn of the stairs and lays a grid across it. Jack steps over it and sits on the top landing with the RAZR open on his knee, because on Ma’s Sundays the call comes after the dishes, and the east stairwell is where Delgado keeps its bars. Down the shaft somebody drags a garment bag along a floor, a door goes, a girl shrieks in a hallway at something that happened last night: the building on the afternoon after a formal.
It rings, and the little outside screen says GLENWOOD.
“Did you eat?” Ma says. “Don’t lie to me, I can hear it in your voice.”

body.text: “Pie, Ma. At the Anchor.”
“Pie isn’t eating.”

body: Behind her the faucet runs, and a pan goes into the rack. “Father Dom did Nazareth at the 8:00,” she says. “A prophet’s never welcome at home. Four minutes. He was good.”
“Father Osei had that one this morning.”
“It’s the Gospel, Jackie. They don’t change it for California.” The faucet goes off. “Your father said *that’s for sure*. In the pew. Out loud.”
“Pop did?”
“Rita Pallante turned around. He looked at her till she turned back.”
Jack leans his head back against the cinderblock. In the wired glass the sun has slid down a row of the wire.
“He came in with me after, to Danny. He told him the Browns are keeping Mangini. Again. Danny put his head down on the table and said bad news is what the mail is for.”
“Ma —”

“It’s Catholic Schools Week, so there were donuts in the hall, and Rita cornered me at the donuts. Was she Catholic. I said she’s baptized. Rita said that isn’t the same thing. I said, *Rita, it’s a start.*” She stops to dry something. “Your father looked at the picture over my shoulder and said *that’s a lot of limes*. Then he went to the garage.”
“It was a taquería, Ma.”
“I looked a long time. She’s tiny. And the writing under it. *Not just friends from school.*” A dish goes into the rack. “Well, I should hope not.”
“Ma.”
“I’m not saying anything. I’m saying somebody should feed her. Gina says it was near midnight out there.”
“It had a heat lamp.”
“I saw the lamp. Rosie wants to know where the crab was.”
“Tell Rosie the crab sends his regards.”

“I’m not telling her that. She’ll want to write him. Nonna’s been saying *Maria Caterina* since the 8:00. She lit another one. That’s two. Father Dom says the candle box needs a refill, and he’s not saying whose fault.”
On Glenwood Avenue the chair scrapes back. Ma says *Gina, I’m not finished*, and Gina says *you’re finished, you’re so finished*, and the phone changes size in somebody’s hand.
“Jack. It’s me. I told him. I waited till he’d had the honey bun, like you said.”
“Good.”
“I said *Mary Catherine* and he said *a NUN?* Like that. Loud. Then I told him about the picture. The lamp, the limes, your face. I did your face.”
“I don’t have a face.”

“You have *the* face. He made me do it twice. Then I read him the writing under it, and he said *spirited debate* means she won. He said *oh, he’s gone.* And then he said — hold on, I have to do his voice — *ask her what she lost the bet for.*”
“What bet?”
“That’s what Ma said! He says you tricked her somehow, it’s the only explanation, and he wants to know how.”
“Tell him I didn’t trick her.”
“He said you’d say that. He said *that’s what a guy who tricked her would say.*”
Jack laughs, and Gina waits for him, drumming something on the table.

“And then he laughed so hard the CO came over. The big one, Jack. Ma put her hand over her eyes. The CO stood there with his newspaper, and Danny said *sorry, sir, family news*, and the CO went back. And Ma said happy birthday early, from all of us, in case your card’s late, and he said late’s a Costigan tradition. Okay. Here. Ma’s reaching.”
“Jackie.”

He hears her take a breath, the Tuesday one, from the bottom of her, and a dish towel come down on the counter. Nothing comes after it. The line holds the faucet and Nonna’s beads in the next room, and it goes on holding them past where a call ought to stop.
“Did you go up today?”

journal.title: Danny Costigan
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; the C.O. reading it first says it’s about a house. The ocean letter got there; Reggie, from Portsmouth, decided on his own the Pacific smells like money and fish. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. On Michaelmas he wrote: Tell Lena hey. I like knowing it. You sound happy out there. Don’t feel bad about it. That’s an order. Lena says hey back. She said it herself. The Saints are four and oh, and she expects him to know that. Third letter, after Columbus Day: the Hopkins got there. He read Ma “Felix Randal” on the phone and she cried; he says he’s telling me so I know he read it, not so I feel bad. The Housman made Reggie cry. Ma told him about Becca. He wants to know if I told Lena hey, or does he have to come out here. I did. He doesn’t know yet. Push-ups: 140. Fourth letter, All Souls: he knows about hey now. ABOUT TIME, up the margin; he wants to know what she said back. Halloween at Trumbull, a guard in a rubber mask. Ma’s getting Nonno a Mass at St. Brigid’s; he wants me to put Nonno in the book here. He says he’d put his in, but he doesn’t have anybody dead. He has the other kind. I wrote him back: she said hey like she meant it. Thanksgiving weekend: put in for a visit for the rich one himself. Liked him in a minute. Reggie waved. Asked which girl. ‘Who’s Flannery O’Connor?’ Noticed I waited till Theo went to the machines. Told Theo he could quit buying. He went to the prison library about Flannery O’Connor. Ma read it to me off an envelope: she raised peacocks and she was mean and he likes her. Is it still something. The Sunday before Christmas I went with Ma; Pop stayed in the truck — the twenty-seventh, he says. Ma took forever at the machines. He said it for me — I’m in love with Lena — and I didn’t tell him he was wrong. Then the rest: the song, the month, Skye. He said he wasn’t going to tell me which one. He said he believes me, both. Then he asked me one question, and I didn’t have an answer. Then he told Ma I miss the beach. Christmas Eve I brought Theo, in the parka. Theo bought; Danny let him. Theo asked if I’d told him about California. Danny said I miss the beach. Asked Theo who comes to see him. “He does.” Christmas, Gina told him about the boat, and he laughed till they cut him off in the middle of a sentence about Lena. Holy Family Sunday, all of us — Pop too. He stood up when he saw Pop. Pop told him they wouldn’t lose. Laughed at the TV one till the guard looked over. Paddle boats: she’s not to know. Asked the table her name, like he didn’t have it. While Ma showed Pop the machines he asked me not to let Pop sit in the truck on the third. Asked Pop about the hall; says the Cruze sounds like a boat. Pop brought him coffee with cream and sugar. He drinks it black. He drank it. Epiphany Sunday, Maria’s Sunday: Pop went in again. Danny stood up. Pop told him the Browns would win, and they did — four straight. Then a letter, in capitals: IS SHE BLIND OR DID YOU LIE. Gina’s yacht got to Trumbull. Sunday, Ma’s Sunday, Gina told him her name across the table at Trumbull and described the taco picture. He said *a NUN?* He said ask her what she lost the bet for. He laughed so hard the CO came over. Ma said happy birthday early in case my card’s late. He said late’s a Costigan tradition.

journal.title: Ma
journal.text: Maria Costigan. St. Brigid’s school secretary. Feeds anybody who comes through the door. Cries at grace every year. Took my phone at the table and counted to eleven without looking at it once. Wrote Becca. December 6th, back from Trumbull: the November bill, four hundred and nine texts. Who is it. I told her a girl. Not Lena. Not nice — something. That’s what Dad said about her. Christmas week: took forever at the machines at Trumbull so Danny and I could talk. Stood Becca’s card at the front of the mantel. Brewed the New Orleans coffee Christmas morning. Put unlimited texting on the family plan; it was cheaper than me. Saw the photos. “Is she Catholic, at least?” When Danny laughed on the phone, she looked at me. Holy Family Sunday she took Pop in. ‘You sit, Frank.’ Showed him the machines. Goes to the seven o’clock on the last day of every year; this year I went with her. Lena called the house on the second of January, and Ma answered, and they talked for ten minutes. ‘She wants you. I don’t know why.’ Now she knows the coffee was hers. At the door she gave me the can back, empty, for the girl who called. From a gas station in Buellton I called her before I said yes on Skye’s phone. She said I was on the phone with Lena all break. I told her Lena’s still got a boyfriend, and he wrote her a song, and it was good. She didn’t say anything. Tuesday Mrs. Pallante called during dinner, and Rosie found it on the Dell before Ma got downstairs. She asked if we got married. Ma didn’t ask me what it was. She asked when I last went to confession. I said tomorrow. Then she said she’d already heard the other thing, when I said hi, so I told her: I think Skye’s the answer. Nonna heard us through the wall. ‘Go tomorrow, Jackie.’ Sunday, after the 8:00 and Trumbull: Father Dom said a prophet’s never welcome at home, and Pop said that’s for sure in the pew. She’d seen the taco picture: *she’s tiny.* Then one question — did I go up today. I said yes. She said good.

choices.text: “I went up, Ma. With her there.”
response: “With her there,” Ma says, trying it. “Did she stay in the pew?”
“She knelt, Ma.”
“Good.” It comes out of her on a long breath, all the way down.
Through the wall Nonna goes on with the decade, and drops the name into it again, *Maria Caterina*, at the end of every Hail Mary, like a bell.

choices.text: “Tell Nonna thank you. For the candle.”
response: “Yes, Ma,” he says. “And tell Nonna thank you. For the candle.”
Ma tells her, with her hand nowhere near the phone: “Mamma, Jackie says thank you for the candle.” From the front room Nonna answers with something short in dialect, and Ma does not translate it.
“Good,” Ma says, about all of it.

choices.text: “Yes, Ma.”
response: “Good.” It comes out of her a half-step higher than anything she has said yet.
The faucet comes on again. “Eat something real,” Ma says over it, and then there is only the water.

s17.slug: SUNDAY · 9:40 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, UPSTAIRS — THE TUB
body: The bath is already run when he gets to the top of the stairs. The bathroom door stands open, and the only light in there is two candles — one on the sill of the open window, one on the floor by the tub’s back foot — and past them the moon coming up over the roofs, still full, or near enough, white across the old tile, black and white hexagons, half of them cracked since before Sol was born. The tub stands in the middle of the floor on four iron claws, deep and white and steaming. Her iPod sits on the edge of the sink in a speaker no bigger than a paperback, turned low: a harpsichord picking its way down over a drum as slow as a pulse, and a woman’s voice somewhere far inside it, too far in to make out a word.
The only other clawfoot Jack has ever known stands on its end in the side yard on Glenwood, painted blue inside, with the Blessed Mother in it and Nonna’s geraniums at her feet.

Skye is in the doorway in a white towel, her hair twisted up off her neck with a pencil stuck through it to hold it. Before he’s off the last stair she puts her hand on his chest, the fingers spread over his sweatshirt, over his heart, and keeps it there, and looks up at him, and says it.
“I watched you go up,” she says. “I kept my word all week. So I’m asking. I want to have sex with you. Tonight. I wanted you to hear it before anything, so you’d know it isn’t the bath talking.”

body.text: “You got there first on Wednesday,” she says. “I’m getting *this* first.”
body.else: “I’m going first this time,” she says.

body: “I heard you,” he says. It isn’t a yes, and it isn’t the other thing, and she nods as if it’s the answer she expected. Her hand stays where it is, and his heart goes on telling it whatever it’s telling it, and she lets it talk as long as it wants.
He looks at her in the candlelight with her chin up and her hand on his heart, and he loves her. It sits in his chest as plain as weather.

She takes the hand back. She lets the towel go onto the bathmat like a towel, steps over the high white side into the water, and sits down in it to her shoulders. “Get in, Youngstown. That’s my second bath. The first one went cold while I practiced.”

He gets out of his clothes by the sink with his back to the mirror — the sweatshirt, the T-shirt, the jeans he wore to Mass with the bulletin still folded in the back pocket — and there’s nothing to it. It’s a bath.
When he steps in and sits down behind her, the water climbs to within a finger of the rim and stops there, trembling, and the two of them hold very still and watch it.
“Archimedes,” she says, not moving.
“He ran down the street after. Naked. Yelling.”
“Del Playa’s seen worse. Don’t tempt me.”

The water is hot enough to sting. The porcelain where it rises out of the water behind him is cold as a church step, and she settles back against his chest between his knees with a long, contented noise, her pinned-up hair against his cheek and the knobs of her spine against his breastbone one at a time. He grew up in a house with one bathroom and two sisters, and nobody in it ever ran him a bath.

“Me first,” she says. She takes his right hand out of the water and puts it on her breast, and takes his left and puts it under the water between her thighs, and holds both of them there under her own. “Like that. Slow. Slower than that — like you’ve got all night. You’ve got all night.”

He does what she tells him. She’s specific about it, low against his jaw — *there*, and *lighter*, and *don’t get clever, just that, keep doing just that* — and after a little she takes her own hands away and leaves it to him. By now he has the rest of it by heart: where her breath catches and what it does when it catches, the way her heel comes up out of the water to hunt for the rim, the moment to change nothing at all. Her weight is all on him, slippery and warm, and every time she breathes he feels it the length of his own chest. The water rocks with her. It laps up the sides and over, and the candle on the floor leans and gutters in the wash, and she pushes back hard against him and comes with her head thrown back on his shoulder and her mouth open at his ear, and a wave of bathwater goes over the rim and across the tile.
When the water settles she says it breathless, against his jaw. “Look at you. You used to be terrible at this.”
She turns her head on his shoulder until her mouth is at his ear. “Your turn. Out loud.”

choices.text: *Tell her exactly what you want. The whole sentence.*
response: So he tells her, start to finish, with his eyes on hers in the candlelight and nothing mumbled to the ceiling: he wants her mouth on him. Here, in the water. Slowly. And he wants to watch her do it.
Skye lifts her head off his shoulder to look at him. “Again,” she says. “The part about watching.”

He says it again. She listens to it like music she paid for. She turns in the water, slopping half the bath onto the floor, and kneels up between his knees with the candlelight on her wet shoulders, and takes him in her hand, and then in her mouth, slowly, her eyes on his face and not leaving it. The rim of the tub is under both his hands before he knows he’s reached for it. The harpsichord goes on picking its way down. She takes the time he asked for and more, until his head is back against the porcelain and her name is coming out of him in pieces — and then, on purpose, short of the end, she stops, and comes up, and wipes her mouth with the back of her wrist.
“Not in here,” she says. “I want the bed for that.”

She stands up out of the bath, and that’s when they find out the water has gone cold. She shivers from her knees to her shoulders and says something about it that would get her fired off *Sweetwater*.

choices.text: *Ask her to stand up and let you look at her.*
response: “Stand up,” he says. “Let me look at you.”

She stands up in the tub with the water running off her. In the candlelight she sets her hands on her hips and her chin up, and waits. He looks as long as he wants, and he tells her what he sees. Not the pose. The water running down the middle of her and pooling in her navel. The gooseflesh coming up along her arms in the air off the window, and her nipples drawn tight with it. The pink line the rim of the tub left across the small of her back. The pencil in her hair, gone crooked, about to fall. A freckle on her hip he has never seen before. Somewhere around the freckle her hands come down off her hips and hang at her sides, and she quits posing and just stands there in the draft from the window and lets him.

He sits up in the water and puts his mouth on her where she stands, his hands on the backs of her thighs to keep her there. She gets one hand in his wet hair. The other goes out and finds the wall, the tile above the soap dish, and braces there, and her knees start to go, and he doesn’t let them; he holds her up and keeps on until she comes with her cheek almost to the tile and his name coming back off it.
When he sinks down again the water closes over him cold — it’s been cold for some time — and she’s shaking.

choices.text: *Ask for the thing you’ve been thinking about since Monday.*
response: “Monday,” he says. “Your mattress. You on top of me with my wrists in your hand, not letting me move.” He keeps his eyes on hers for the rest. “I’ve thought about it every day since. In the Commons. At the Anchor, holding a pie.”

She makes a low sound at the back of her throat. She turns over in the water and kneels up between his knees, takes both his wrists in one hand and lifts them over his head to the high back of the tub, and pins them there against the cold porcelain. Her other hand goes under the water. “Don’t move,” she says into his ear, and he doesn’t, and she takes him in her fist under the water, slow and then not slow, her breasts slick against his chest and her mouth at his ear telling him exactly how still he’s being, how good he is at it, how much longer he’s going to have to be, and the bath goes over the rim in a wave and drowns the candle on the floor with a hiss. He pulls at her grip without meaning to. She tightens it and doesn’t stop —
— and stops. Lets go of his wrists. Sits back on her heels in water he only now notices has gone as cold as the Channel.
“Bed,” she says. “Now. You’re turning blue.”

s18.slug: SUNDAY · 10:30 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM — THE NO
body: Her bed is the mattress on the floor under the open window, and the moon comes in over the sill and off the white wall onto the sheet, enough to see by and no more.

body.text: She finishes what she started in the tub. She’s unhurried about it now, kneeling over him in the light off the wall with her hair coming down out of the pencil around her face, no water to fight and nothing to brace against, and she makes it last. When he comes it’s with her name in his mouth — both of her names, *Skye* and then the other one, the one from the taquería, never said in a bed before now. She goes still. Then she puts her face down on his stomach and says it too, the whole thing, every syllable, into his skin, like a title she’s won.

It’s her turn to look. She puts him on his back in the light off the wall and kneels beside him and takes as long as he did — longer — and doesn’t tell him one thing she sees, and he finds out from the other side what that costs. Then her mouth on him, unhurried, with her hand spread low on his stomach to keep him down on the sheet, until he comes under it, her name breaking in the middle on the way out of him.

She puts him on his back and lays his hands palm down on the mattress on either side of his head, and lets go of them. “You keep them there,” she says. “I’m not doing it for you this time.” Then her mouth: his throat, the notch of his collarbone, a slow line down the middle of him, her tongue at his navel, her wet hair dragging cold behind it over his chest, and then she takes him into her mouth, unhurried, with her eyes up on his face to see if his hands have moved. They haven’t. His fingers are dug into the sheet to the knuckle. He tells her, in a voice he doesn’t recognize, that he can’t, and she lifts her head just long enough to say *yes, you can*, and he does. He keeps them there through all of it, the heat and the slow pull of her and her hand closed at the base of him, until he comes with his back up off the mattress and both fists full of sheet and her name torn in half on the way out.

body: After that there’s no order to it and no hurry, and nobody’s turn. They trade, out loud now, both of them. “Turn over,” he says, and she does, and he puts his mouth to the small of her back and works down from there, the backs of her thighs, the crease behind one knee, telling her low where he’s going a sentence before he gets there, so she has to wait for it. She makes him do the whole length of her like that. “Now you,” she says, when he’s back up beside her on the pillow. “Your hand. Slower than that. And don’t you look at the ceiling. Look at me.” He looks at her. He asks for hers on him at the same time, and gets it, and for a long while the two of them lie face to face on one pillow, working each other slowly with their eyes open, and neither of them looks away.

body.text: Then she does a thing he would never have known to ask for. She lies back with her knees up in the light off the wall and puts her own hand between her legs, and tells him to watch, and to say what he sees, the way he did in the bath. So he does — her stomach drawing tight, the color climbing her throat, her free hand finding his wrist and gripping it — and she comes slow and long and nearly quiet with his voice going on at her ear, rolling up through her, her heel pushing at the sheet.
body.else: Then he goes down on her in the light off the wall with her knees up and her fingers in his hair, and this time she hardly directs him at all; now and then she says his name, low, to check he’s still there. When she comes it’s slow and long and nearly quiet, rolling up through her, her heel on his shoulder and her stomach trembling under his hand.

body: Somewhere in there he finds the pencil, under his back, and she takes it out of his hand and throws it at the window.

Later — he couldn’t say how much later; the moon has gone some way along the wall — she’s over him. Her knees on either side of his hips. Her hands on his chest. Her hair all the way down now. Nothing on either of them, anywhere. She lowers herself along him until she’s lying on him from hip to breast, and there’s no air left between their bodies but in one place, and he can feel that one place exactly: the wet heat of her right there, a breath away from where all of him is straining up toward it, so near it’s hardly a distance at all. They’ve never been this close. Above him she has gone completely still. His hands are on her hips, his fingers spread over the bones of them, and they’re what’s holding it — his own two hands, keeping the last inch where it is while every other part of him argues with them. His forearms are shaking. Her breasts are against his chest and her heartbeat is going into him through them, fast, and the light off the wall is in her loosened hair, and he can feel how little it would take — not a decision, hardly a motion, just his hands opening.
She’s breathing hard. She puts her mouth beside his ear.
“Jack,” she says, into his ear, with her eyes shut. That’s all. She asked at the top of the stairs.

He doesn’t say anything. The surf comes up through the window and goes out again. A car goes by on Del Playa with its windows down and takes its radio with it. Her breath is on his neck, fast and then slower. Under his hands the long muscles of her hips tremble with holding still, and his hands don’t move.
In the silence he sees the aisle this morning: the walk back from the altar with the taste still in his mouth, and her in the pew ahead of him on her knees, not looking at him, looking at the altar.
“It’s still no,” he says. “For now.”
She goes on breathing against his neck. He knows how that sounds, and he won’t sand it, so he says the rest.
“But it’s closer than it’s ever been.”

She lifts her head to look at him, her face just over his in the moonlight off the wall, close enough that he can see her eyes go from one of his to the other. He has one reason left, and she’s owed that too.

choices.key: Sunday night Skye asked, first, before anything. You told her it’s still no, for now — but closer than it’s ever been — and that the only thing holding it is that you went up this morning.
response: “I went up this morning,” he says. “That’s all that’s holding it.”
She goes very still on him. Her hands come up off his chest and stay in the air above him, open, touching nothing.

choices.text: *Tell her what you want, all of it. Then the no.*
choices.key: Sunday night Skye asked, first, before anything. You told her everything you want — and then that it’s still no, for now, but closer than it’s ever been.
response: So he tells her what he wants, all of it, the man from the tub who can say things now. “I want this,” he says. “Tonight, with nothing in the way. I want to wake up here. I want to quit counting days. I sat next to you this morning and wanted you between the readings, and I went up anyway, and I wanted you the whole way back down the aisle.” He doesn’t round any of it off. Then the no again, in the same voice, and the reason: he went up this morning.
She puts her forehead down on his collarbone and keeps it there, and he feels her breathe out against his chest, long, down to the bottom of her.

choices.text: *Say it into her mouth. Don’t let go of her.*
choices.key: Sunday night Skye asked, first, before anything. You said no into her mouth — for now, closer than it’s ever been — and didn’t let go of her.
response: He pulls her mouth down to his and says it again into it, the no and the rest, with his hands still on her hips and holding: not letting her go, and not letting her one hair nearer. She kisses him through every word of it, hard, and his hands stay exactly where they are.
She bites his lip, not gently, and keeps her teeth there while she breathes, and he can taste the bath on her. He bites her back.

s18a.slug: SUNDAY · 10:50 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM — TO THE LETTER

body.text: “This morning,” she says. “That’s what’s holding it.” She counts something on his chest with one finger. He’d bet it’s the days to next Sunday.
“You said all that,” she says into his collarbone, “and then you said no.” She lifts her head. She’s smiling.
“You bit me back,” she says. “That’s new.” She touches her lip.

body: “That was a no,” she says. “I heard it. It just had its car keys out.”
She tries his line in her own mouth, slowly, to hear what it sounds like there. “*Closer than it’s ever been.*” She doesn’t get off him.
“Love is patient,” she says. “A girl in a navy skirt read it at me this morning. So now it’s official.”
“She read it at everybody.”
“She was looking at me.”
“Everybody looks at you.”
“Not like that. Like she was reading me my lines.” She leans down until her nose is against his and her eyes are too close to focus on. “I liked them,” she says. “I’m keeping them.”
“So,” she says. “What does the letter say?”
He tells her. It doesn’t take long, and she listens to all of it with her nose against his, and when he’s done she nods, once, like a woman reading a contract she has decided to sign.

She keeps the letter. She stays where she is, astride him, and his hands stay where they are, and the distance he named stays exactly what it was — and inside it she starts to move. Against him, never onto him: slow at first, the long slide of her along him and back, wet and hot and maddeningly patient, her palms spread on his chest and her eyes open on his, finding out how much there is to do in the room he’s left her. There’s a great deal. He finds that out too. She rocks and he rises to meet her and his hands hold and hold, his wrists aching with it and his fingers sunk in the give of her hips, and she starts to say something in Corinne’s vowels and loses it halfway, and then it isn’t slow. The sheet is gone somewhere off the end of the mattress. The damp has come up at her temples, and then she bends to him and her hair falls around both their faces and closes them in, and in the dark of it they breathe each other’s breath, mouths open and not kissing, until she comes with a sound into his mouth and he goes with her, between them, against her stomach, never inside her, the two of them shaking together, his hands still on her hips and still holding.

Afterward they come apart. She slides off him onto her side and lies with her knee over his and her heart still going against his arm. While they weren’t looking the moon has come down off the wall, and it lies on the floorboards now among their clothes.

s18b.slug: SUNDAY · 11:45 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM — THE QUESTION
body: It’s as dark in the room as it gets with the window open on Del Playa: the moon on the floor, a streetlight down at the corner, the white of the sheet. The lamp is off. The candles in the bathroom have burned down or drowned; he can’t smell them anymore. She’s lying on his chest with her ear over his heart, drawing something on his ribs with one fingernail. He’s decided it’s the state of Ohio. It turns out, when he asks, to be a horse.
“Gina was telling your brother today,” she says. “You said. What did he say?”
“Gina told him across the table,” he says, and feels her go still to listen. “He said, *a NUN?*”

Skye laughs so hard she has to roll off him and put her face in the pillow to keep it off the street. When he gets to the CO coming over she comes up for air, and when he gets to the bet — Danny wants to know what she lost it for — she goes back in.
She comes up out of the pillow wiping her eyes with the heel of her hand. “What *did* I lose the bet for?”
“He wants to know.”
“Tell him I’m still deciding.” She settles back down on him, her cheek on his chest again. “I like your brother.”
“He thinks I must’ve tricked you somehow.”
“Into what?”
“Any of it.”
She thinks that over with her chin on his breastbone. “Tell him it was the flannel,” she says.

She’s quiet after that, her ear back over his heart, long enough that he thinks she’s gone to sleep. “It’s slow now,” she says at last, about the heart. “It was very fast before. I was keeping track.” The fingernail goes back to the horse. The surf comes up through the window, and a gust off the water lifts the curtain and lets it down.
“What was the question?” she says. “The one I’m the answer to.”
She doesn’t lift her head. The fingernail has stopped on his ribs, wherever the horse’s heart would be.
He gives her Nonna’s.
“She asked me what makes me pray.”
The fingernail doesn’t move.
“Do I?”
“Yes.”

It’s true. He prays for her at red lights, in the space between the red and the green. He has prayed for her by name. And this morning on his knees beside her, with the Host still on his tongue, he said her name again — both of them, now.
“What do you say?” she says. “When you do it. For me.”
“A Hail Mary. Your name. Then whatever I want for you that day.”
“Like what?”
“That you sleep. That your mother calls less.” He thinks about it. “That Corinne gets a cold.”
Her head comes up. “You pray for Corinne to get a cold.”
“A small one. Over a weekend.”
She puts her head back down, and he feels her smile against his chest, and then he feels it go.
“You’re going Wednesday,” she says.
“Yes.”
“And you have to tell him you won’t do it again. That’s the rule. The purpose part.” She waits until he says yes to that too. “And then you come back here.”
“Yes.”

“I’m not mad at it.” She says it fast. “I want you to know that. I came to your Mass. I knelt. I’d do it again next Sunday, I’d do it every Sunday, I liked it, I liked watching you go up. That isn’t the part.”
She comes up on one elbow, and he can see the shine of her eyes in the dark and not much else.
“So here’s mine,” she says. “When it’s yes —”
*When*, she says, and he doesn’t correct her.

“— am I only ever going to be something you carry into that little room on a Wednesday?” Her voice doesn’t go up at the end. “You go in and say me to a man behind a screen, and he tells you what I cost, and you come out, and you get to go up on Sunday. And I’m still here. I’m always still here.”

body.text: “I can live in the daylight column,” she says. “I told you I could. But this isn’t daylight, Jack. I’ll be in the bad column on a Wednesday every week of my life with you.”
body.else: “I’ll be the thing you tell him about on a Wednesday,” she says. “Every week of my life with you.”

body: She’s quiet. Her heart is going against his ribs, fast for somebody lying still.

“Monday I didn’t finish something,” she says. “I said I didn’t want to be the occasion. I had the rest of it right there, and I put it back, because it wasn’t ready.” She takes a breath. “It’s ready.”
“I want to be the good thing,” she says. “With the lights off.”
The lights are off.

There’s one answer in him. It has a priest in it, and a Wednesday, and a church she knelt in this morning for his sake and may only be visiting. He can’t put that in her hands at midnight in the dark with nothing on and call it an answer. She’s waiting. He can hear the surf, and her breathing, and his own heart under her ear, and none of it is going to say anything for him.

choices.text: “You’re the good thing. You’re the good thing *now*.”
choices.key: In the dark Skye asked what question she’s the answer to, and said she wants to be the good thing with the lights off. You told her she’s the good thing now.
response: She doesn’t answer. Her hand comes looking for his in the dark, and finds it, and brings it down and holds it on her stomach, under her own, like in the bath, only now there is nothing she wants him to do with it. Her thumb goes back and forth over his knuckles, slowly, like she’s counting them to be sure they’re all there.

choices.key: In the dark Skye asked what question she’s the answer to, and said she wants to be the good thing with the lights off. You told her you don’t know how yet — you’re trying to find out.
response: “Okay,” she says. “Find out fast.”
She puts her head back down on his chest. After a moment, smaller, into his skin: “I mean it about fast.”
And later, when he thinks she’s asleep: “Anybody else I know would’ve had an answer. A good one. I’d have believed it for a week.”

choices.text: “Then we’ll have to keep the lights off.”

response: She laughs, and then she doesn’t, and then she turns over with her back against his chest and pulls his arm over her and holds it there by the wrist.
“That was a good one,” she says, with her back to him. “I’m going to need a better one.”

body: She falls asleep first. He feels it happen, her breathing going long against him and her hand going heavy where it lies, and just before she’s gone she says one more thing.

“Fast,” she says, already mostly gone.
“Lights,” she says, already mostly gone, and doesn’t finish it.

body: Her hair against his mouth smells of the bath and the candles. The moon is going west off the floor, leaving the boards to the dark a little at a time. His jeans are where he dropped them by the mattress, with the RAZR in the pocket. Downstairs Tomás’s stereo has been off for an hour, and the house is down to its own noises: the old refrigerator in the kitchen, the wind trying Sol’s swing on its chains out on the porch. Delgado is a long cold walk up Ocean Road, and she is warm all down his side, and her mouth has come a little open against his shoulder, and in what light there is he can see the crease the pillow is starting on her cheek.

body: She walks him down. She goes ahead of him on the stairs in his flannel and nothing else, buttoned wrong, past Tomás’s dark door and across the front room and out onto the porch, and at the top step she stops with one hand on the post. Sol’s swing is moving a little on its new chains in the wind off the water.

body.text: “Like last time,” she says, and pulls the flannel together at her throat. “I liked last time. Go before I quit liking it.”
body.else: “Go home, Youngstown,” she says, and pulls the flannel together at her throat. “Before I change my mind about letting you.”

body: He goes down the steps. When he looks back from the street she’s still up there, a pale shape in the dark of the porch with the flannel pulled shut.

He goes up Del Playa with his hands in the pocket of his sweatshirt — a couch on somebody’s lawn, a porch light left burning, a cooler tipped over in the gutter, the surf under the bluff louder than it ever is by day — and turns onto Ocean Road. St. Brendan’s is dark on the hill, the bell tower black against a sky the moon has washed almost white, the doors shut on the place where he knelt this morning. He knows it’s there without looking.
Under a streetlight on Ocean Road he opens the RAZR. Three he never heard: one from before midnight, two from after one.

body: Nonna is up with her beads before the furnace, then. It’s after four on Glenwood.
Room 412 is dark, and Theo is awake in it. He’s on his back in his bed with the blanket to his chin, and in the light from the hall Jack can see that his eyes are open.
“Home,” Jack says.
Theo says nothing at all. His eyes stay on Jack in the dark while Jack gets his shoes off, and while he gets into bed, and after.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. s19s.slug: MONDAY · 12:55 AM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM
body: He stays.

He lies on his back in her bed with nothing on either of them and her asleep against him, and sleep is all it is; he keeps it to that. Her knee is over his. Her hand is open on his chest where it fell, and now and then the fingers move a little, still drawing horses. The moon has gone off the floor, and the window is full of it instead, and the curtain lifts in the air off the water and settles again. He isn’t tired at all.
He says a Hail Mary for her under his breath, the red-light kind, fast, with her name on the end of it. And another, slower, for Danny, whose birthday is Tuesday.
She stirs. She doesn’t open her eyes. Into his shoulder, half asleep, she says, “Mary Catherine says goodnight.”
“Goodnight,” he tells her. Both of them.
She smiles without waking, or he thinks she does; in the dark he can’t be sure of anything but the weight of her, and the warmth, and her breath going slow against his collarbone.

On the floor by the mattress his jeans buzz against the boards. He reaches down one-armed without waking her, fishes the RAZR out of the pocket, and opens it low against his chest so the screen won’t find her face. One from before midnight he never heard, and two just now.

body: It’s after four on Glenwood. The furnace won’t have kicked on yet, and Nonna is up in the dark at the kitchen table with her beads.

He leaves Theo’s where it is. He closes the phone and puts it back in the jeans and lies down again, and Skye turns her face into his shoulder in her sleep. Her hand on his chest closes a little, around nothing, like a sleeping kid’s hand on a finger.
